text: National Cooperative Database jk"Vªh; lgdkjh MsVkcsl lgdkfjrk ea=ky; Ministry of Cooperation Hkkjr ljdkj Government of India National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report सहकारिता मंत्ालय Ministr y of Cooperation भा ि त स ि का ि Gov ernment of India ii National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report cooperatives.gov.in National Cooperative Database Help Desk Email : ncd.techcoop@gmail.com T elephone No. : 011 – 20862616 Address : Atal Akshya Urja Bhawan, CGO Complex, Pragati V ihar, New Delhi, Delhi -110001 iii iv v vi PREFACE vii PREFACE In pursuit of our goal to consolidate and facilitate access to the consolidated and latest information on cooperative societies nationwide, the Ministry of Cooperation, in collaboration with States/ UTs Registrar Offices, Federations, NCUI and District Nodal officers has developed the National Cooperative Database (NCD). This user-friendly platform serves as a centralized hub, offering comprehensive insights on about 8 lakh Cooperative Societies. The NCD features an intuitive user-friendly dashboard with detailed analytical reports that plays a pivotal role in policy planning and decision making for the stakeholders involved in the cooperative domain. The NCD portal assist in identifying gaps in the geographical distribution of Cooperative Societies and provides vital information on cooperative linkages, both vertically and horizontally for informed decision-making. This report, titled "National Cooperative Database Report- 2023," goes beyond presenting mere data sets. It includes insightful information and detailed analysis of major sectors such as PACS, Dairy, Fishery, Housing, Labour, Credit & Thrift, Cooperative Banking etc. Additionally, the report delves into the status of cooperatives registered in each State/UT, providing district-wise details accessible through the Portal. We aim to offer stakeholders in the cooperative sector a valuable resource through this comprehensive report. The authentic and up-to- date data presented on the Portal, serves as a cornerstone for informed decision-making for the stakeholders. We trust that this database will prove to be instrumental in serving the interests of all the cooperative sectors across the nation. Shri Pankaj Kumar Bansal, IAS Additional Secretary Ministry of Cooperation viii EXECUTIVE SUMMARY viii T he Cooperative Movement in India, deeply rooted in the principles of cooperation and reflective of the ancient philosophy of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam,' has undergone a transformative journey. From its humble beginnings marked by voluntary efforts, it received legal recognition in 1904 with the Cooperative Credit Societies Act. Post-independence, cooperatives were strategically integrated into national development plans, with an emphasis on collaboration with village panchayats. The establishment of key institutions like the National Cooperative Development Cooperation (NCDC) and the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) played a crucial role in providing financial support and guidance. The recent formation of the Ministry of Cooperation in 2021 underscores the Government's commitment to fostering cooperative growth. Operating on principles that prioritize people over capital, cooperatives contribute significantly to inclusive economic growth, empowering marginalized communities across sectors such as agriculture, credit, housing, and more. This cooperative model has become a vital component of India's socio- economic development, aligning with the Nation's strategies for inclusive growth and empowerment. The Ministry of Cooperation had a vision to deepen the cooperative movement, establish a cooperative-based economic model, and connect every village with cooperatives for overall prosperity. Ministry has embarked on a transformative journey with a primary focus on fortifying the cooperative movement through a visionary initiative - the National Cooperative Database (NCD). This database aims to fill a critical gap by providing comprehensive and up-to-date information on the extensive network of cooperatives in the country. Recognizing the need for collaboration, the Ministry has actively engaged various stakeholders like States/UTs Cooperation Departments, National Federations, States Federations, line Ministries of the Central Government and all other stakeholders at various level. Several committees like the Steering Committee, Advisory Committee and Project Management Group were setup to streamline the development of the NCD. The phased approach to data collection, starting with primary cooperative societies in agriculture, dairy and fisheries sectors, demonstrates a strategic and meticulous approach. The NCD is not merely a repository; it’s a dynamic tool connecting with other databases, ensuring real-time updates. The Ministry’s commitment to transparency and efficient collaboration is evident in its efforts to link the NCD with various databases, facilitating seamless information flow. Financially backed by the Cooperatives Education Fund, this initiative underscores the Ministry’s broader objective- fostering prosperity and equitable development at both the grassroots and ix National levels. It symbolizes a paradigm shift in cooperative governance, emphasizing transparency, collaboration, and data-driven decision-making for a more resilient and prosperous cooperative sector in India. The National Cooperative Database (NCD) is an essential online platform capturing and organizing information on 8.0 lakh+ registered Cooperative Societies having membership of more than 29 Crores. It acts as a pivotal link between the Central Ministry and States/UTs, providing detailed contact details for all registered societies, including names, addresses, phone numbers & emails for seamless electronic communication. With user-friendly access to comprehensive cooperative information, the portal ensures secure login-based access for stakeholders. Its analytical tools, reporting modules and query options empower users with data-driven insights, facilitating informed decision-making. The portal's geographical spread maps and GIS data representation help pinpoint coverage gaps. Additionally, NCD plays a crucial role in addressing credit gaps, fostering networking among cooperatives, identifying funding opportunities, and supporting training initiatives. In summary, the NCD is a dynamic hub that promotes collaboration, facilitates informed choices, and contributes to the sustainable growth of the cooperative sector. The National Cooperative Database (NCD) provides a comprehensive view of the diverse cooperative landscape in India, revealing its extensive reach across various sectors. All the 8.0 Lakh cooperatives have been categorized among 29 Sectors. In the agricultural domain, the Short- Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) comprises 1,03,304 Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) and 351 District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs). For long-term rural credit, the operation involves 14 State Co-operative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs). The report encompasses a wide array of cooperative entities, including Credit and Thrift Societies, Urban Cooperative Banks, Dairy Cooperatives (1,41,807), Fishery Cooperatives (25,649), and 26,798 Primary Agriculture and Allied Cooperatives. Significant roles are played by Labour cooperatives, consumer cooperatives (21,067), and marketing cooperatives (9,121). In the housing cooperative sector, there are 1,91,734 societies, while 44,545 labour cooperatives and 19,576 Handloom Textile & Weaver Cooperative Societies address specific needs. The sugar sector sees the involvement of 281 cooperatives, and there are 22,735 Primary Agro Processing/Industrial Cooperatives. Livestock cooperatives (16,677) and 24,261 Women Cooperatives (with 54.27 lakh members) ix x make essential contributions to the cooperative network. Altogether, this extensive cooperative network significantly propels India's socio-economic development, illustrating the robust and diverse nature of cooperative engagement across the nation. This spirit has been ingrained in our culture, driving socio-economic reforms at the grassroots level. The International Cooperative Alliance (ICA) defines cooperatives as enterprises owned, controlled, and run by and for their members, emphasizing their role in meeting common economic, social, and cultural needs. Cooperatives, prioritizing people over capital, play a crucial role in fostering community business sense, enhancing social bonds, and contributing to inclusive economic growth. Despite challenges, especially in finances and governance, cooperatives empower marginalized communities by providing livelihoods, education, and market access. Recognizing their significance, the Ministry of Cooperation (MoC) was formed on 6 th July, 2021, with a vision to deepen the cooperative movement, establish a cooperative- based economic model, and connect every village with cooperatives for overall prosperity. 1.2 Indian Cooperative Movement Even before formal cooperative structures came into being through the passing of a law, the practice of the concept of cooperation and cooperative activities were prevalent in several parts of India.Village communities collectively creating permanent assets like village tanks or village forests called Devarai or Vanarai was fairly common. Some of them were named as Chit Funds, Kuries, Bhishies, Phads. In the Madras Presidency were organised ‘Nidhis’ or Mutual-Loan Associations. In the Punjab, a society on cooperative lines was started in 1891 for controlling the common land of the village for the benefit of the co-sharers. All these efforts were purely voluntary and strictly non-official. The Cooperative Movement in India emerged out of the distress and turmoil that prevailed in the last quarter of the 19 th century. The Industrial Revolution left the hands of a mass population and drove them to agriculture. Agriculture, at that time, was the only source of employment and livelihood. The consequent sub-division and fragmentation of holdings made agriculture uneconomic. Many factors such as the rigidity of land revenue collection, uncertainty of rainfall and consequently lesser crop production compelled the farmers to approach the moneylenders. The moneylenders advanced some money either by purchasing their crop at throwaway price or charging a high rate of interest. All these factors emphasised the need for the provision of cheap credit through an alternative agency. The history of Cooperative Movement in India can be divided into two phases. First, cooperative Movement in the Pre-Independence era and second in the Post-Independence era. I. Cooperative movement in the Pre- Independence Era Cooperatives became legal entity way back in 1904 in India with the introduction of the “Cooperative Credit Societies Act”. It mentioned the norms for the constitution of cooperative societies, their 4 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report membership, registration, liabilities of members, and disposal of profits, rulemaking power and dissolution. This Act was restrictive in some manner as it kept non-credit and other societies out of its field. Subsequently, the defects of the 1904 Act were remedied when the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 was enacted and it widened scope for the cooperatives as marketing societies, handloom weavers and other artists societies. In the year 1914, the Maclagan Committee proposed certain reforms in the cooperative societies especially for the credit societies and it proposed a three-tier cooperative banking at Centre, Province and District levels. The Government of India Act, 1919 empowered the provinces to make law for cooperatives, The Bombay Cooperative Society Act, 1925 was the first cooperative legislation passed by the provincial government. The GoI enacted the Multi-Unit Cooperative Societies Act, 1942 for promotion and regulation of cooperatives having membership from more than one province. The Act delegated the power of the Central Registrar of Cooperatives to the State Registrars for all practical purposes. II. Cooperative Movement in the Post- Independence Era With Independence, a different and a new form of government came to rule. It was the government of the people, by the people and for the people. It was also felt that there was need for a conscientious drive to promote people’s voluntary participation in planning and implementation of all programs, which were connected with the economic development, so that economic power is decentralized and economic development and social justice can take place simultaneously. After Independence cooperatives became an integral part of India’s Five-Year Plans. The First Five-Year Plan designated a crucial role for cooperative organizations, emphasizing their coordination with village panchayats. Another important event of this period was the publication of the report of the Committee of Direction of the All-India Rural Credit Survey in 1954. The establishment of the National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC) under the National Cooperative Development Corporation Act, 1963, marked a crucial statutory initiative. Another significant milestone in credit development was the inception of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) in July 1982 during the Sixth Plan period. The Seventh Plan aimed to ensure adequate financial support for weaker sections and less developed areas. The Indian Parliament passed the Multi-State Cooperative Organisations Act in 1984 to consolidate laws governing similar societies. To consolidate the numerous laws governing the same kinds of societies, the Government of India announced a National Policy on Cooperatives in 2002. Currently, the MSCS Amendment Act 2023 and MSCS Amendment rules were created to match the current laws with the 97th Amendment part IX(B) of India’s constitution. The aim is to enhance governance, increase transparency, and implement structural changes among the MSCS. Recent policy changes like the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act and upcoming National Policy empower cooperatives with greater independence to the cooperative. The Ministry of Cooperation, established on 6 th July, 2021, has significantly boosted the cooperative movement by implementing various schemes and initiatives. The Ministry is responsible for establishing a unique administrative, legal, and policy framework for advancing the cooperative movement across the nation. The MoC's main initiatives include facilitating the growth of Multi-State Cooperative Societies and streamlining procedures for “Ease of Doing Business” for cooperatives. Its focus is on strengthening and modernizing cooperatives, promoting transparency and computerization, fostering competitiveness, and ensuring accessible development for underprivileged rural communities. The ultimate goal is to connect every village with cooperatives, fostering prosperity 5 lgdkfjrk ea=kky; Ministry of Cooperation through the mantra of 'Sahakar se Samriddhi ,' ultimately contributing to the nation’s overall prosperity. 1.3 All India Cooperat ives Cooperative societies in India represent a distinctive socio-economic framework profoundly ingrained in the nation’s fabric. Rooted in principles of democratic governance, equitable distribution of benefits, and voluntary associations, these societies serve as catalysts for inclusive development across various sectors. From rural and agriculture credit to consumer welfare and industrial collaborations, cooperative societies play an integral role in fostering collective enterprise and addressing their members’ diverse needs. A prominent feature of cooperative societies is their emphasis on democratic decision-making, ensuring that every member has a voice in the governance and operations of the organization. This participatory approach fosters a sense of ownership and promotes transparency and accountability within the cooperative structure. In India, cooperative societies span across diverse sectors, including Agriculture, Credit and Banking, Housing, Women's Welfare, amongst many. They act as vital conduits for financial inclusion, offering credit facilities to farmers, and small entrepreneurs who might otherwise face challenges accessing traditional banking services. Additionally, these societies contribute significantly to rural development by empowering local communities and mitigating socio-economic disparities. In recent years, the Indian Government has revitalized and strengthened the cooperative sector through policy initiatives and financial support. Various schemes and subsidies have been introduced to encourage the formation and growth of cooperative societies, particularly in rural areas where they play a vital role in agricultural development. Under the vision of ‘Sahakar se Samriddhi’, Ministry of Cooperation has taken prominent steps in promoting and coordinating cooperative activities across the nation. Presently, India boasts 29 primary cooperatives, namely, Agro-Processing/Industrial Cooperatives, Bee Farming Cooperatives, Consumer Cooperatives, Credit and thrift Society, Dairy Cooperative, Educational and training Cooperatives, Fishery Cooperatives, Handicraft Cooperatives, Handloom Textile and Weavers Cooperatives, Housing Cooperative Society, Jute and Coir Cooperative, Labour Cooperatives, Livestock & Poultry Cooperatives, Marketing Cooperatives, Miscellaneous Credit Cooperatives, Miscellaneous Non-Credit Cooperatives, Multipurpose Cooperatives, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), Sericulture Cooperatives, Social Welfare & Cultural Cooperatives, Sugar Mills Cooperatives, Tourism Cooperatives, Transport Cooperatives, Tribal-SC/ST Cooperatives, Urban Cooperative Banks (UCB) and Women's Welfare Cooperatives. Cumulatively, these cooperatives have 8,00,203 societies with a 29,12,80,275 membership count. PACS, Dairy and Fishery Cooperatives have been instrumental in strengthening the rural sectors. These cooperatives provide farmers access to credit, technology and markets, thereby enhancing their productivity and income. Additionally, they facilitate the collective procurement of inputs and the marketing of produce, giving farmers a stronger bargaining position in the market. The Agriculture/Allied Cooperatives, with 76 federations, have 98,36,270 members with 26,797 society count. Gujarat has the highest society count (6,643) in this sector followed by Madhya Pradesh (3,742) and Maharashtra (3,474). Notably, Uttar Pradesh has the highest membership (56,49,109), followed by Maharashtra (9,93,065) and Madhya Pradesh (7,00,666). As far as Fishery cooperatives are concerned, there are 25,609 societies with 46,74,279 members. Telangana has the highest number of societies (4,985), followed by Maharashtra (3,403) and Madhya Pradesh (2,798). 6 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report Agro-processing / Industrial Cooperatives, with 22 federations, have 22,735 societies count with a membership of 25,31,349. Maharashtra has the highest number of societies (5,288), followed by Uttar Pradesh (4,025) and Punjab (1,987). Maharashtra has the highest membership count (12,53,407), followed by Karnataka (4,58,625) and Gujarat (2,14,407). The Dairy Cooperative sector with 73 federation, have 1,41,807 societies with 1,56,87,794 members. The highest Dairy cooperatives are recorded in Uttar Pradesh (17,985), followed by Karnataka (17,645) and Gujarat (16,346). Notably, Gujarat has the highest membership count (36,39,508). Livestock and Poultry sector has 16,677 societies and 13,39,349 members. Telangana state has the highest number of Livestock and Poultry societies (7,974) with 7,48,441 members. Cooperative Banks and Credit Societies play a crucial role in promoting financial inclusion. They cater to the banking needs of individuals in rural and semi-urban areas, offering various financial services, including savings, credit, and insurance. These institutions significantly reduce the dependency on traditional moneylenders and empower individuals with limited access to mainstream banking. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) with 11 federations are operational in 1,502 societies. Notably, Maharashtra, with 428 UCBs and 60,21,811 membership count, boasts the highest number, followed by Karnataka, with 279 societies having 23,35,863 members, and Gujarat with 187 societies and 14,91,531 members. The Credit and Thrift Cooperatives have a membership of 4,32,75,731 in 79,999 societies. Telangana records the highest number of societies (24,024), while the highest number of memberships is recorded in Maharashtra (2,27,27,861). Miscellaneous Credit and Non-credit Cooperatives have 5,575 and 30,364 societies respectively. They are having 89,19,537 and 25,05,838 members respectively. Maharashtra records the highest number (7,073) of miscellaneous non-credit societies, while the highest number of members (8,59,093) are associated with societies in Karnataka. The Miscellaneous credit has a maximum number of societies (3,238) enrolled in West Bengal, with Karnataka having highest membership count of 52,80,248. Miscellaneous credit sector has 21 federations whereas Miscellaneous non-credit has 96 federations across the State/UT. There are 1,03,725 Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) serving to its 13,99,27,330 members. Maharashtra leads with 20,949 societies, followed by Gujarat (10,248) and Bihar (8,463). Notably, Kerala has the highest PACS membership (2,56,28,261) followed by Bihar (1,36,08,525). The cooperative movement in India has also expanded into sectors such as housing, handlooms, and consumer goods. Housing Cooperatives enable members to collectively address their housing needs, particularly in urban areas where affordable housing is a pressing concern. The cooperatives have 1,46,65,027 members in 1,91,734 societies. Maharashtra has the highest number of housing cooperatives (1,25,734), followed by Gujarat (29,529). Housing Cooperative sector has 47 federations/unions registered across the states/UTs. Handloom Cooperatives support traditional artisans, preserve indigenous crafts, and provide a platform for sustainable livelihoods. The handloom textile and weaver cooperatives have 51,56,723 members in 19,576 societies. Manipur has the highest count (5,588) of societies, followed by Uttar Pradesh (1,841). Markedly, the highest membership (29,85,671) is in Karnataka, followed by Tamil Nadu (3,01,969). The Jute and Coir Cooperatives have 56 societies with 5,755 members. Karnataka has the highest number of societies (17) in this sector. Another prominent cooperative, the Consumer Cooperative, has 21,067 societies registered with 63,75,920 members. Noteworthily, Madhya Pradesh (4,959) has the highest number of societies under consumer cooperatives, followed by Chhattisgarh (2,417). The highest number 7 lgdkfjrk ea=kky; Ministry of Cooperation of members is recorded in Madhya Pradesh (12,53,231), followed by Maharashtra (10,61,516). The consumer sector has 30 federations/unions registered across the State/UT. Other notable cooperatives, such as Sugar Mill Cooperatives, are a specific type of cooperative societies which operate in the sugar industry. The cooperatives aim to empower farmers by giving them control over the processing and marketing of sugarcane, ensuring fair returns for the produce. There are 284 cooperative societies in this sector with total 47,83,246 members. Maharashtra has the highest number (94) of sugar mill cooperatives with 16,27,196 members, followed by Karnataka and Bihar, both having 35 societies under the cooperatives. Sericulture Cooperatives and Beekeeping Cooperatives are specialized cooperative societies focusing on silk production and beekeeping, respectively. The Sericulture Cooperatives has 67,149 members in 498 societies. Karnataka has the highest count of societies (97), followed by Odisha (54). Notably, highest membership of 31,608 is recorded in Odisha. The Bee farming cooperatives have 325 societies with 38,181 members. Bihar has the highest society count (124), followed by Manipur (85). The highest membership of 13,956 is recorded in Rajasthan, followed by Karnataka (10,988). Both cooperatives contribute to rural livelihoods, environmental conservation, and the sustainable production of value-added products. Educational and Training Cooperatives are specialized cooperative entities that provide skill development, education, and training programs. These cooperatives are crucial in providing education and training opportunities, particularly in communities with limited resources. These Cooperatives have 78,717 members enrolled in 387 societies. Maharashtra records the highest number of societies (73), followed by Rajasthan (63). Notably, Maharashtra has the highest members count (32,533), followed by Assam (13,746). The cooperatives have 78 federations/ unions registered across State/UT. Women's Welfare Cooperatives promote women’s well-being and empowerment through cooperative principles. These cooperatives address women’s socio-economic challenges, incorporating education, healthcare, economic empowerment, and social support. The sector has 24,261 societies with 54,21,424 members. Madhya Pradesh has the highest count of cooperatives (11,073), followed by Rajasthan (4,218) and Assam (2,885). Notably, Telangana has the highest number of registered members (30,96,825), followed by Rajasthan (6,23,324) and Assam (6,18,927). The Social Welfare and Cultural Cooperatives address social, cultural, and community-oriented objectives. The cooperatives aim to enhance their members’ well-being and contribute to society’s overall development. All India Cooperative sectors record 2,055 social welfare and cultural cooperatives with 2,91,308 members. Telangana and Maharashtra register the highest society count, i.e., 1,095 and 424, with 2,00,666 and 31,523 members, respectively. Another distinguished society benefiting the tribal sectors is Tribal SC/ST Cooperatives. The cooperatives aim to empower SC/ST and tribal populations by providing them access to resources, economic resources, and a platform for collective decision-making. The cooperatives have 10,33,894 members in 1,472 societies. Chhattisgarh has the highest count of cooperatives (847), followed by Punjab (255) and Haryana (80). The highest membership count of 7,63,886 is recorded for Chhattisgarh. This cooperative sector has 3 federations. Labour Cooperatives embody the principles of self-help, equity, democracy, and solidarity among workers. The cooperative emphasizes the collective well-being of its members while striving for sustainability and economic viability. The cooperatives have 14,91,300 members enrolled in 44,545 societies. Maharashtra 8 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report represents the cooperatives’ highest membership (3,77,278), followed by Gujarat (3,43,376). These cooperatives have 65 federations registered across states/UTs. Transport and Tourism Cooperatives play a significant role in fostering economic growth while safeguarding the local cultures and well-being of communities. There are 4,163 registered societies in Transport sector, while tourism sector records presence of 459 societies across the country. Haryana registers the highest number of societies (1,935) in transport with a membership of 4,87,181. Haryana is followed by Jharkhand with 259 society count, while in membership Maharashtra has the second highest membership of 58,638. Maharashtra leads with 125 societies in tourism, followed by Meghalaya (55) and Andaman and Nicobar Islands (46). Maharashtra boasts highest count on memberships (2,15,908), followed by Andaman and Nicobar Islands (53,529). Multipurpose Cooperatives are characterized by the ability to operate across multiple domains, addressing a range of social, economic, and cultural requirements within a community. The flexibility and adaptability of multipurpose cooperatives make them effective for community- driven progress. There are 19,964 cooperative societies in this sector with 25,82,130 members. Maharashtra has the highest number of cooperatives (4,656), followed by Karnataka (3,387). Karnataka leads in the membership (1471891), followed by Maharashtra (3,65,173). Marketing Cooperatives are specialized cooperative entities that focus on promoting and selling the products or services of their member businesses. These cooperatives are formed by individual producers, farmers, or businesses to jointly market their products, reduce costs, and improve their bargaining power in the marketplace. Marketing cooperatives have 45,90,611 members associated with 9,121 societies. Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of societies in the sector i.e., 1,791 followed by Gujarat with 1,713 societies. Tamil Nadu has the highest number of members (8,85,211), followed by Maharashtra (6,75,050) and Karnataka (5,41,030). Ministry of Cooperation 1.5 Multi-State Coope rative Societies The Multi-State Cooperative Societies (MSCS) are those cooperative societies whose objects and operations are not confined to one State and they serve the interests of their members in more than one State for their economic and social betterment in accordance with the cooperative principles. These societies are registered under the Multi- State Societies Act 2002. The Act has been recently amended and such provisions have been incorporated in the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 that ensures and facilitate the functional autonomy and democratic functioning as well as improving governance, transparency and efficiency in management of societies registered under this Act. The amended provisions facilitate the establishment of a Cooperative Election Authority, creation of a Cooperative Rehabilitation Reconstruction and Development Fund, appointment of Cooperative Ombudsman and Information Officers, and representation of women and SC/ST members on cooperative societies boards. The MSCS are involved in diverse economic activities in various sectors of economy such as Fishery, Dairy, Industrial, Marketing, Housing, Health, Transport, Labour, Farming, Credit, Service, Producer and Processing, Consumer, Handloom & Handicraft etc. At present about 1607 Multi-State Cooperative Societies are registered and functioning under the MSCS Act catering to sector specific needs of their members. Report 23 lgdkfjrk ea=kky; Ministry of Cooperation Journey of National Cooperative Database 2.1 Introduction India has a rich history of cooperatives and our forefathers have tried to instill and nurture the spirit of cooperation in every citizen. Cooperation has remained our way of life in India, which advocates ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam [the world is one family] from time immemorial. India resides in its villages and they function on the principle of cooperation to capitalize on various socio-economic and people centric reforms for a better future. The word 'Cooperation' signifies team trusteeship and elucidates two terminological assertions – saha and karya, meaning working together. The International Cooperative Alliance (ICA) defines Cooperatives as people-centered enterprises owned, controlled, and run by and for their members to realise their common economic, social, and cultural needs and aspirations. Cooperatives function as people-centric organizations with immense capacity to generate and absorb social capital. They prioritize people over capital, brings cohesiveness, community business sense and enhance social bonding. Cooperatives, both worldwide and in India have significant potential to ensure all- inclusive economic growth. In India particularly, cooperatives empower marginalized communities despite facing challenges like limited finances and governance issues. Their role in providing livelihoods, education, and market access is crucial. Strengthening financial resources, governance, and fostering collaboration among cooperatives are essential for maximizing their impact and advancing equitable development. The subject of cooperation was earlier being administered through the Cooperation Division of the erstwhile Department of Agriculture, Cooperation & Farmers Welfare. By a decision of the Union Cabinet and through the notification dated 6th July, 2021, a new Ministry – the Ministry of Cooperation (MoC) was created. The MoC aims to deepen cooperative movement and reach upto the grassroots and develop a cooperative based economy model to realize “Sahakarita se Samriddhi” and to provide a separate administrative, legal and policy framework for strengthening the cooperative movement in the country. It aims to foster genuine people-based cooperatives at the grassroots level, promoting a cooperative-based economic model where members work responsibly. The Ministry’s core activities include streamlining business processes for cooperatives to enhance Ease of 'Doing Business (EoDB)' and facilitating the development of Multi-State Cooperative Societies. Its focus is on strengthening and modernizing cooperatives, promoting transparency and computerization, fostering competitiveness, and ensuring accessible development for underprivileged rural communities. The ultimate goal is to connect every village with cooperatives, fostering prosperity ultimately contributing to the nation’s overall prosperity. India is home to around 8 lakh cooperatives, out of which around 80% are non-credit cooperatives, such as textiles, hospitals, services, industrial, producer, processing, dairy, fisheries, sugar, marketing, consumer, labour, housing, etc., and 20% are credit cooperatives. Today, cooperatives 24 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report have a presence all over the country having more than 29 crore members. In last two years, since the formation of Ministry of Cooperation, the cooperative movement has been strengthened due to several path-breaking initiatives of the Ministry. One of the initiatives is creation of National Cooperative Database in coordination with States/UTs Government. The comprehensive national database will comprise data of various kinds of cooperatives–from the lowest unit of the cooperative sector, that is, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) to national-level institutions. By systematically verifying the grassroots presence of cooperatives, this sector is becoming more streamlined and effective in its operations. This revolutionary initiative not only facilitates the identification of active cooperative societies, but also assists the Government in the formulation of policies to strengthen the cooperative sector to elevate the standard of living for the underprivileged and marginalized sections of society. 2.2 Need for Database Despite India being home to almost 25% of total cooperative societies in the world and with history of cooperative movement in India dating back to more than a century, there was no comprehensive, authentic and updated data repository in the country about cooperatives, their activities, their members, their financial details etc. The availability of organized database of the cooperatives, can help in formulating programs and schemes, mentioning the exact number of beneficiaries. The Ministry of Cooperation was constituted on 6th July, 2021 with a mandate, inter alia to strengthen cooperative movement in the country and deepening its reach up to grassroots; and creation of appropriate policy, legal and institutional framework to help cooperatives realize their potential. To fulfil this mandate, the process for developing a National Cooperative Database was initiated by the Ministry in consultation with the State/UT Governments, National Cooperative Federations, Central line Ministries and all other Stakeholders at various levels. 2.3 Scope & Benefits of National Cooperative Database The objective of developing National Cooperative Database (NCD) is to provide: • A single point access to authentic and updated information on cooperatives of different sectors and develop a process for better understanding of cooperatives. • The database will function as the main planning tool for Central Ministries, State Governments, Cooperative Federations, Cooperators and Sectoral Institutions like NABARD, etc., for cooperative sector. • The database would also bring synergy among various databases maintained by Central line Ministries and State Governments. • It would also help in identifying gaps/ vacuums in geographical distribution of cooperatives in the country and establishing upward/downward linkages of cooperative societies (Primary to Apex). The National Cooperative Database (NCD) captures data on several parameters related to cooperatives i.e., location details, number of members, economic activities, their upward and downward linkages, level of operations, assets and liabilities, etc. It involved development of a web based secure system to facilitate data feeding from each of the district registrar/functional registrar office which can be viewed and verified by respective state registrar office. By adopting latest IT Tools and Management Information System (MIS), NCD is available on real-time basis to all stakeholders and can easily be adopted for various activities over a period of time. 25 lgdkfjrk ea=kky; Ministry of Cooperation 2.4 Consultations wit h Stakeholders The need for a comprehensive database was discussed and agreed upon in various forums, leading to the finalization of data attributes through extensive consultations with states, federations, and central ministries. The project received inputs from 53 stakeholders, showcasing a collaborative effort to shape the National Cooperative Database. Based on inputs received, sector specific data fields and online forms were developed. Hon’ble Minister of Cooperation accorded in principle approval of the project during a presentation made before him on 30th September 2022. 2.5 National Cooperative Union of India’ s contribution in the development of National Cooperative Database: Earlier National Cooperatives Union of India updated state and sector-wise cooperative data on a regular basis for the publication of its Indian Cooperative Movement-Statistical Profile. After the Ministry of Cooperation decided to create a National Cooperative Database on cooperatives, NCUI actively collaborated with the Ministry of Cooperation to develop the National Cooperative Database (NCD). Leveraging its expertise, NCUI's National Cooperative Databank Division (NCDD) plays a vital role in formulating data collection templates and providing insights for efficient data gathering, and supports the National Database Team by contributing to drafting chapters and compiling data for the NCD report. NCUI facilitate the process by creating user IDs for Nodal Officers and Interns/DEOs engaged in data entry and also ensures timely payment of stipends/honorariums of the Interns/DEO(s) and Nodal officers engaged for the data entry of the societies in the NCD portal. NCUI provides invaluable support from the very inception of the NCD project, right through to its successful completion. 2.6 Organizational Structure for Developing Database: The overall work is being carried under the guidance of Secretary (Cooperation). Following operational structure has been put in place; • Steering Committee under Chairmanship of Additional Secretary (Coop) & CRCS was constituted for monitoring of progress and implementation of strategy for development of National Cooperative Database. The members of the Committee is from MoC, PMG, NCDC (LINAC), NCUI & AICTE. • Advisory Committee under Chairmanship of Additional Secretary (Coop) & CRCS was constituted for getting inputs from various stakeholders such as State RCS, National Cooperative Federations and Statutory Bodies (NABARD, NDDB, NFDB). • Project Management Group (PMG) was set up under Chief Project Officer and Ex-DDG (NIC) who is responsible for architecting the portal for National Cooperative Database. PMG has designed and developed the software solution and has been spearheading its implementation across states. Regular meetings of Steering/Advisory Committees and PMG were held to sort out technical & administrative issues, on priority basis, at every stage of database development. Secretary (Cooperation) also reviewed the progress regularly and held frequent meetings with State RCs, National Cooperative Federations & Steering Committee. 2.7 Activities and Fun ding of Project • Development of sector-specific Web Forms by software development team for collecting data from Primary to Apex cooperative society. • Exhaustive repeated training for Data Entry Operators (DEOs) and Nodal Officers at district level. • Collection of data from District Registrar Offices of State RCS and functional registrars 26 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report in different sectors through interns/ DEOs. • Verification and correction of each and every record for all field officials. A module was developed wherein the district nodal officers submitted certificates on completion of verified entries. • Cross validation of data from State RCS, St.CB, DCCB, NABARD, NDDB, NFDB, NAFSCOB, NCDFI & FISHCOFED. • Documentation of software application and technical flows, Standardization of Master code, user manual and training manual. • Development of Analytical Dashboard, MIS Reports, Graphical Presentations, GIS Maps to show coverage under various Cooperatives, Query Based Reports and Multiple Level of User Access through User Management Module. • The expenditure on procuring hardware & software, engaging IT Professional & Interns/DEOs, etc. for National Cooperative Database has been met through Cooperative Education Fund (CEF). 2.8 Data Collection fo r Database in Phased Manner Keeping in view the diverse nature and size of cooperative sector, it was decided to create the database in a phased manner. Phase-I: Under Phase-I, mapping of about 2.64 lakh primary cooperative societies of three sectors i.e., Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS), Dairy and Fisheries was completed in February, 2023. Under this phase, in addition to staff at district registrar offices services of 560 local interns enrolled on portal of All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) were onboarded for data entries at District Registrar Offices. Phase-II: Under this Phase, Mapping of National Cooperative Societies/Federations along with their General Body Members was completed. Further, their downward linkages with State Federations, District Unions and Primary Cooperative were also established. The data related to StCB, DCCB, UCB, SCARDB, PCARDB, Sugar Cooperative Mills, State Federations, District Unions and MSCS were collected directly from cooperative societies or through their National/State Federations. Phase-III: Under this Phase, Ministry of Cooperation initiated the process of extending the National Cooperative Database to remaining more than 5 lakh cooperative societies working in all other sectors, through the office of RCSs of State/UTs. Almost all States/UTs have completed data entry under National Cooperative Database. By November 2023, the data of around 8 lakh primary cooperative societies has been uploaded on the National Cooperative Database by the nodal officers of States/UTs. The total number of members engaged in these cooperative societies are around 29,12,80,275. 2.9 Linkage with other Databases A central project has been formulated for the automation of cooperative registration and management processes in the offices of the Registrar of Cooperative Society of States/ UTs. The process has been initiated to have API-based linkages of the software system that is being developed for use at state and district-level registrar offices with the National Cooperative Database (NCD). This will ensure the real-time updating of data on the National Cooperative Database about registration of any new cooperative society as well as updation of other data items in respect of existing cooperative societies. NCD, being centralized platform of all sectors of cooperatives, depending on the sectoral parameters, it is important to create live linkages with other databases of central departments and state IT systems which will help in seamless updation of data on respective sectoral activities to build analytical layers for planning purpose. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. These banks were one of the first sources of institutional credit to the farmers in our country. Banks are unique in the sense that their functioning is inherently driven by values viz. equality, open and voluntary association, democracy, mutual support, self-reliance, non- exploitative operations etc. which are mostly absent in other forms of credit institutions. District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) stand at the second tier in the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) having State Cooperative Banks (StCBs) at the State/ Apex level and Primary Agriculture Credit Cooperative Societies (PACS) at the village level. DCCBs come under the regulatory purview of RBI through Banking Regulation, Act, 1949 (AACS). Sector-wise Cooperatives L ong-term rural credit cooperatives were established for providing funds for investment in agriculture – including land development, farm mechanisation and minor irrigation - rural industries and housing. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. They play a very significant role in meeting credit needs of poor and marginalized sections of the society. They offer customized loan products and repayment schedules based on members’ needs and income levels and foster a sense of community and social responsibility among members. In India, there are 79,795 primary credit and thrift societies in 34 States, except for Ladakh and Kerala, with 4.32 crore members. Out of 79,795 societies, 66,713 societies are functional, 10,489 are dormant and 2,593 are under liquidation. Around 56% societies i.e., 44,404 are operating in urban areas and the remaining 35,391 societies are operating in rural areas. Telangana and Maharashtra have the maximum number of credit and thrift societies. Approximately 55% of the total primary credit and thrift societies are operating in these two states alone. The remaining 45% of the societies are operating in 32 states. Telangana state has the highest number of societies i.e., 24,020 with a membership base of 47.77 lakh followed by Maharashtra which has 20,337 societies with 2.27 crore members. The core functions of these societies are: • Thrift : Encouraging members to save regularly through deposits, often with attractive interest rates compared to traditional savings accounts. • Credit: Providing loans to members for various purposes like education, medical expenses, business ventures, or agricultural needs, often at lower interest rates than commercial banks. • Other Services: Many societies offer additional services like micro-insurance, money transfers, and financial literacy programs. The term Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs), though not formally defined, refers to primary cooperative banks located in urban and semi-urban areas. UCBs are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act of 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Ministry of Cooperation, in coordination with the Reserve Bank, has initiated reforms to strengthen the cooperative banking structure. The vision guiding the framework is to consolidate their position as friendly neighbourhood banks by catering to the heterogeneity in the customer base, while offering more operational flexibility to strong UCBs in order to enhance their contribution to credit intermediation Over a period of 120 years of their existence, Urban Cooperative Banks are successfully serving the society and meeting banking needs of their customers and members. Being local banks, they are the preferred friendly “Neighbourhood banks of Choice” as they provide doorstep banking services to their customers. The National Cooperative Database (NCD) records 1,335 Urban Cooperative Banks in the country. Around 63% of these banks are located in 3 states namely Maharashtra, Karnataka and Gujarat. The State of Maharashtra tops the list with 428 banks having 60,21,811 members, followed by Karnataka (279) having 23,35,863 members and Gujarat (187) having 14,91,531 members. In view of their importance in providing credit to the poor and weaker sections of the society, the RBI is giving focused attention for strengthening the sector. The Hon’ble Minister of Home and Cooperation, Shri Amit Shah has given a vision to have one UCB in each town of India, so that these UCBs can meet growing credit needs of MSMEs and help in economic Non-Credit Cooperative Societies 4.8 Dairy T he Dairy Cooperatives in India has experienced a remarkable growth, positioning the country as the global leader in dairy production. On a significant note, the dairy cooperative model has emerged as a pivotal force in boosting the nation’s economy. The sector predominantly driven by smallholder farmers is overseen at the National level by the key organizations like the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) and the National Cooperative Dairy Federation of India (NCDFI). NDDB, founded in 1965 under Dr. Verghese Kurien (the milkman of India), spearheaded transformative initiatives such as the White Revolution and Operation Flood, fostering dairy cooperatives, improving milk production, and empowering farmers through a cooperative model. This involved the introduction of modern technologies, infrastructure development, and robust marketing strategies. The NCDFI, on the other hand, is a National Federation of Cooperative Dairies that coordinates, networks, and advocates for the working of these cooperatives. Structured in a multi-tier system, the dairy cooperatives feature a vast membership, including over 1.5 crore farmers, with significant female representation. Across India’s 36 states/union territories (UTs), there are 1,41,221 dairy cooperatives. Among these, 1,00,844 are functional, 30,166 are non-functional, and 10,211 are in the process of liquidation. Most dairy cooperatives (1,37,507) are operational in the rural areas, while only 3,714 cooperatives have their presence in urban areas. The dairy sector collectively boasts a membership of 1,56,55,580 individuals. Around 30% gram panchayats i.e., 81,566 out of 2,69,503 gram panchayats are covered under Dairy cooperatives. Karnataka leads in the number of dairy cooperatives with 17,514, followed by Gujarat (16,319) and Maharashtra (13,533). Gujarat also stands out with the highest membership count of 36,37,966 followed by Karnataka with 32,37,337 members. Currently, around 72.3% (i.e., 1,02,003) dairy cooperatives are affiliated with federation, or union. The diversification of dairy products, including butter, ghee, cheese, yogurt, and milk powder, has increased income for both cooperatives and farmers and enhanced the sector’s competitiveness. To meet domestic and international market demands, concerted efforts are underway to improve dairy products’ quality and safety standards. Dairy cooperatives have embraced technological advancements such as bulk milk coolers and automated milking machines to enhance the efficiency of collection, processing, and distribution. The outlook for the cooperative dairy sector is promising, driven by the rising demand for dairy products and a strategic focus on digitalization and e-commerce to achieve further operational efficiency and reach a broader consumer base. Intriguingly, the Cooperative Dairy sector stands as a fundamental pillar of India’s Dairy industry, contributing to economic growth and serving as an exemplary model for sustainable agricultural The inception of the fishery cooperatives movement dates to 1913 with the establishment of the ‘Karla Machhimar Cooperative Society’ in Maharashtra. Significantly, the Fishery sector plays a vital role in the Indian economy, by supporting the livelihoods of fishers and fish farmers. To bolster the Indian economy through the fisheries sector, the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) was launched in 2019-20 by the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry, and Dairying. In 2018-19, a dedicated fund, i.e., the Fisheries & Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund (FIDF) of ` 2,552 crore was established. The initiation of the Blue Revolution, 2014 aimed to increase fish production and develop infrastructure within the fisheries sector. The Ministry of Cooperation’s formation prioritizes fisheries cooperatives, with plans to organize them in each panchayat. The apex cooperative organization for developing the Fishery cooperatives movement in India is the National Federation of Fishers’ Cooperatives Ltd. (FISHCOPFED), registered in 1980. It is dedicated to empowering fisheries cooperatives and is affiliated with international bodies. As per National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal, India has 25,535 primary fishery societies with nearly 46.73 lakh fishers as members, including exclusive fisherwomen cooperative societies. Telangana has the highest number of fishery cooperative societies (4,985) followed by Maharashtra (3,403). Notably, NCD depicts coverage of 25,061 gram panchayats under fishery cooperatives and 10,471 fishery cooperatives are affiliated with banks, unions, or federations. The fishery cooperative sector significantly enhances vulnerable groups’ livelihoods, nutritional status, and social security, benefiting around 4 million people in India. Agriculture sector contributes around 18.3% towards the Gross Domestic Product (GDP). It also provides employment opportunities to about 44% of the working force. The sectors allied to the agriculture sector are fishery, horticulture, animal husbandry, dairy farming, poultry and milk production. Any changes in the agriculture sector have a large effect on the country’s economy. The biggest industries like textiles, food processing, milk, jute, and sugar all depend on agriculture to obtain the raw material. In India, there are 26,375 Primary Agriculture and Allied Cooperatives, 4 State Level Federations, 33 District Level Federations (Regional level federations are included) and 26 Block/Taluka/Mandal Level Federations with total membership of 98,07,968. Out of total cooperatives, 16,857 are functional, 7,498 are non-functional/dormant and 2,020 are under liquidation process. Around 89% of the cooperatives (23,378) have their presence in rural areas and the remaining 11% (2,997) cooperatives are registered in urban areas. Major Agriculture and Allied States with highest number of registered cooperatives are Gujarat (6,617), Madhya Pradesh (3,725) and Maharashtra (3,473). Uttar Pradesh State has the highest number of members (56,43,958) followed by Maharashtra (9,93,005). Apart from a significant contribution to the country’s GDP, agriculture and allied sectors provide raw materials to the industrial sector and serve as market for industrial products. Generally, a greater number of labours are required for construction of buildings, roads, factories and dams. Cooperative labour societies eliminate the middlemen and thus save labour from exploitation. The evolution of labour cooperatives in India has become a significant force in driving economic development, particularly in sectors like agriculture, handicrafts, handloom, and small-scale industries. These cooperatives, regulated by the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act. of 2023 and the state-specific Cooperative Societies Act, embody the principles of democratic ownership and decision-making, where workers have equal stakes and actively participate in significant decisions through one-member, one- vote system. Government support, including various schemes and programs, is directed towards encouraging the formation and growth of cooperatives as tools for social inclusion and economic empowerment. As per the National Cooperative Database (NCD), there are 44,362 registered labour cooperatives with 14,85,006 members. Currently, 28,096 societies are functional, 11,544 are non-functional, and 4,722 are under liquidation. The urban and rural areas have 15,668 and 28,694 cooperatives respectively. Around 16.8% (7,452) societies are affiliated with federations/unions. Maharashtra leads in the number of cooperatives (11,271), followed by Haryana (9,508) and Telangana (4,296). Maharashtra also tops the list in terms of registered members (3,77,237), followed by Gujarat (3,43,332) and Haryana (1,49,158). There are 4 state level federations, 56 district level federations and 2 regional level federations. Notably, Labour Cooperatives are pivotal in addressing socio-economic challenges, emphasizing collective ownership, democratic decision-making, and equitable benefits among workers. However, their growth faces constraints such as limited access to finance, management issues, and competition from conventional business models. 78 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report common economic, social, and cultural needs. Its objective is to work for its members, like purchasing lands to construct the residential buildings for their members. Housing units that have been facilitated by housing cooperatives have certain unique features. Not only they are planned developments but they also provide various infrastructure supports such as local shopping centres, community centres, banks, parks, playgrounds, schools, etc., thereby subscribing to the development of integrated and sustainable human settlements. The grass-roots level primary housing cooperatives are affiliated to the State level “Apex Cooperative Housing Federations (ACHFs)” which are functioning in various States and Union Territories. The National Cooperative Housing Federation of India (NCHF), set up in the year 1969, is the umbrella organization of cooperative housing movement and engaged in promoting, coordinating and facilitating the operations of the ACHFs and housing cooperatives to enable them to provide affordable houses to their members. The Housing Cooperative in India is a strong, noble and popular movement which has witnessed mass participation over the years. The National Cooperative Database projects the total number of Housing Cooperative Societies in the country as 1,91,657 having a total membership of 1,47,06,694. Around 92% (1,76,224) societies are operating in urban areas. The state of Maharashtra has the highest number of cooperatives i.e., 1,25,886 followed by Gujarat (29,363) and West Bengal (6,729). Maharashtra state has the highest number of members 70,90,973 followed by Tamil Nadu having 19,84,745 members. There are 13 state level federations, 23 district level federations and 8 block/taluka/mandal level federations. The key feature of housing cooperatives is constructing low cost and affordable houses. Further, houses constructed through housing cooperatives comply with the requirement of local building regulations. marketing organizations are associations of producers for the collective marketing of their produce and for securing for the members the advantages that result from large-scale business which an individual cultivator cannot secure because of his small marketable surplus. These cooperatives are a cooperative business model where members pool their resources, such as crops, livestock, or other agricultural products, and work together to improve their bargaining power in the marketplace. This aggregated volume allows the cooperatives to negotiate better terms with buyers, processors, or distributors. Marketing Cooperatives provide farmers with improved access to markets that may be difficult for individual producers to reach. This is especially important for small-scale farmers who may not have the resources to market and distribute their products independently. By combining their resources and operations, members of a marketing cooperative can benefit from economies of scale. National Cooperative Database provides the number of Marketing Cooperative Societies presently registered in the country as 9,104 with a total membership of 46,35,383. Out of which, 7023 marketing cooperatives are functional, 1,795 are non-functional, and 286 are under liquidation. Currently, Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of Marketing Cooperatives (1,791), followed by Gujarat (1712) and Maharashtra (990). Tamil Nadu has the highest number of members i.e., 9,24,669 followed by Maharashtra (6,74,057) and Karnataka (5,41,004). There are 14 state level federations and 63 district level federations (includes regional federations). Marketing Cooperatives play a multifaceted role in boosting the Indian economy, particularly in the agricultural sector, by enhancing market access, reducing risks, promoting value addition, and empowering farmers. Indian handloom sector is ancient and has served the economy well in terms of employment. The relevance of the handloom sector in the agrarian economy is massive because of its linkages with crucial and sensitive sectors like Agriculture. It uses agricultural products as raw materials and, therefore, provides an ever-ready market for agricultural produce. As per National Cooperative Database, there are total 16,089 primary cooperative societies registered under this sector with a membership of 48,26,425. More than 50% (8,988) of cooperatives have their presence in rural areas. The state of Manipur has the highest number of these societies i.e., 2,090 followed by Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu having 1,841 and 1,351 societies respectively. The societies in Karnataka are serving to highest number of members i.e., 29,69,088 while the societies in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra have 3,01,969 and 2,65,399 members respectively. There are total 10 state level federations and 6 district level federations under this sector. Handloom, Textiles and Weaver sector directly addresses women’s empowerment. The handloom sector is largely household-based, carried out with labour contributed by the entire family. Therefore, the engagement of a large number of women in any capacity under this sector has ensured direct remunerations for them, thus empowering them through financial independence and improved Hence, the scope of the agro-processing industry encompasses all operations from the stage of harvest till the material reaches the end users in the desired form, packaging, quantity, quality and price. In India, there are 22,341 Primary Agro Processing / Industrial Cooperatives, 7 State Level Federations, 11 District Level Federations and 1 Block/Taluka/Mandal Level Federation with total membership of 24,74,786, out of which 9,071 are functional, 9,239 are non-functional/ dormant and 4,031 are under liquidation process. Out of total, 11,561 cooperatives are registered in urban area and 10,780 are registered in rural area. Major Agro Processing/ Industrial States with highest number of registered cooperatives are Maharashtra (5,292), Uttar Pradesh (3,969) and Punjab (1,987). The cooperative societies in Maharashtra constitute the highest number of members i.e., 12,53,521 followed by Karnataka (4,53,612) and Gujarat (2,13,089). India being an agrarian economy, processing of agricultural produce is of vital importance and an important segment of the Indian economy in terms of contribution to GDP. It not only helps in value addition, but also in employment generation and exports of agri- produce. The key sub-segments of the Food Processing industry in India are Fruits & Vegetables, Poultry & Meat Processing, Fisheries, Food Retail, Dairy Industry, etc. 104 National Cooperative Database 2023 : India’s Livestock industry is the largest in the world and is primarily dominated by smallholder farmers, making the cooperative model a vital force in its development. The livestock cooperatives in India are represented by Animal Husbandry Department of the states monitored through State level Federation or State Livestock Development Board. The Livestock cooperatives in India work under vertically integrated three tier structure i.e, State Level Federation followed by District Level Unions and Primary Level Societies. As per National Cooperative Database, there are 16,033 primary level societies comprising 13,20,465 members. Around 90% (14,462) of the societies have their presence in rural areas while remaining 1,571 societies are catering to urban areas. Telangana leads in the number of livestock cooperatives with 7,974 societies, followed by Andhra Pradesh (1,627) and Karnataka (865). Telangana also stands out with the highest membership count of 7,48,441 followed by Karnataka (1,74,613) and Gujarat (79,657). In conclusion, the cooperative in livestock sector in India has come a long way, significantly contributing to the country’s economic growth and the welfare of its rural population. It continues to evolve and adapt to the changing market dynamics, making it a cornerstone of India’s livestock industry and a model for sustainable agricultural development. 108 National Cooperative The sectors in which these cooperatives operate are as diverse as the women themselves. In India, there are 24,264 women cooperatives in 28 State/UT at primary level with 54.27 lakh members. Out of 24,264 women cooperatives, 20,491 are operating in rural areas which are 84% of the total women cooperatives. The remaining 3,773 are operating in urban areas. Telangana has the highest number of members i.e., 30,96,825 followed by Rajasthan (6,34,247) and Assam (6,18,674). Most of the affiliated cooperatives have their presence in Madhya Pradesh (207) and Bihar (205). Women cooperatives are operating in various sectors like dairy, farming, jewellery making, handicrafts, and even IT services. Further, it has been observed that cooperatives operating in tourism sector are only 46, but they have highest percentage of members (37%) followed by labour cooperatives (26.78%). https://cooperatives.gov.in Profile T here are two Acts in existence pertaining to the regulation of the Cooperatives in Andhra Pradesh out of which A.P. Cooperative Societies Act VII of 1964 is the older Act, the provisions of this act are considered necessary for such cooperatives which are dependent on the support from the Government and consequential intervention in the governance. However, even this Act has been substantially amended in the year 2001, duly aiming at promoting the cooperatives in accordance with the principles of cooperation and at reducing the Government control to some extent. The second Act is A.P. Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies (MACS) Act of 1995, which aims at promoting self-reliant, responsible, accountable and autonomous Cooperative Societies with their own Bye-laws, which would make the Cooperative Movement more vibrant. As per data available on National Cooperative Database, there are 17,659 Primary Cooperative Societies,12 Multi-State Cooperatives, 9 State Federations and 13 District Cooperative Banks in the state of Andhra Pradesh. About 13,556 primary cooperatives are functional and notably, majority (about 80%) of primary cooperatives are registered in rural areas. Anantapur and SPSR Nellore districts have the maximum number of primary cooperatives. There are 2,135 fishery cooperatives, 2,047 PACS, 1,627 livestock and poultry cooperatives, 1,527 labour cooperatives and 812 dairy cooperatives. Importantly, 2,047 PACS are having 67,27,240 members i.e., around 70% of total members, whereas fisheries membership is only 2,73,902 i.e., only 2.8% of the total number of cooperative members in the state. - please visit the NCD Portal at: https://cooperatives.gov.in Profile A runachal Pradesh is basically an agrarian state, 66% of the total working population is engaged in agriculture and other allied activities. Initially, the State had adopted the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912. Subsequently, State enacted its own Law “The Arunachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act, 1978 and Arunachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Rules, 1982”. At present all the cooperative societies are registered in the State of Arunachal Pradesh under the said Act and are governed under the provisions of the Arunachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act, 1978 and Arunachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Rules,1982 made thereunder. The State Government has chosen cooperative institutions as a means to overcome the prevailing difficulties and were assigned with full responsibilities for implementation of Public Distribution System (PDS) from the early 1980s. The Cooperative Movement proved its worthiness by successful implementation of PDS in the state which was rated as best in the country during 1990. The total number of Primary Cooperative Societies functioning in 25 districts is 1,166 having a total membership of 87,549. The number of Multipurpose Cooperative Societies and Agriculture & Allied Societies are 468 and 172 respectively which have made these sectors most prominent in the State. Papum Pare district has the highest number of Multipurpose Cooperative Societies (240) and Kurung Kumey district has the highest number of Agriculture & Allied Societies (67). Handloom Textile & Weavers Cooperatives are catering to the highest number of members (31,657) through 57 societies. The State Government is planning to promote the Cooperatives in Tourism and Education sectors as well. The cooperatives have now started to provide Home-Stay facilities for the tourist and to show case the traditional way of life and provide local food and drinks (Specially in the Ziro valley of Lower Subansiri District and Tawang District). Rural areas are deprived of good and proper education. Education cooperative societies are being promoted to impart quality education to the students with reasonable amount of admission and tuition fees in the state of Arunachal Pradesh. These cooperative schools also impart computer education in rural areas. information - please visit the NCD Portal at: https://cooperatives.gov.in Profile T he cooperative societies in the state are overseen by the Registrar of Cooperative Societies. The governing legislation includes, the Assam Cooperative Societies Act, 2007 (Act IV of 2012), Assam Rajiv Gandhi University of Cooperative Management Act, 2010, Warehousing Corporation Act, 1962, the Assam Cooperative Land Mortgage Bank Act, 1960, and the Assam Money Lenders Act, 1934. Assam has a total number of 10,978 Primary Cooperative Societies, out of which 6,136 are currently operational, 4,095 non-functional, and 747 under liquidations. Across 35 districts, a comprehensive membership of 43,19,974 has been registered. Notably, Nagaon leads with 765 societies and the highest membership of 2,70,709, followed by Udalguri with 527 societies and a membership of 1,38,247. The Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS/FSS/LAMPS) with 1868 societies holds maximum number of membership (28,74,110), covering almost 79% of the Gram Panchayats. The State comprises of 908 Dairy Societies, 845 Livestock and Poultry and 600 Fisheries Societies. 75.9% of the PACS, 18.4% of dairy and 3.8% of fishery society are affiliated with banks, federations/unions. A noteworthy aspect is the significant presence of the Women’s Welfare sector, constituting 26.2% of the societies, reflecting the substantial involvement of women and their pivotal role in the state’s GDP upliftment. Cooperative Societies have played a vital role in economic upliftment of people, particularly of the weaker sections, in rural areas of the state. The state has undertaken various initiatives to organize and strengthen these societies. More than 26,000 cooperative societies have been registered under various sectors such as Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), Dairy Cooperative Societies, Fishery Cooperatives, Handloom Textile and Weavers Cooperatives etc. As per National Cooperative Database, there are 26,640 Primary Cooperatives working in the state with about 1.6 crore members. Around 18% (4,763) of the societies are registered in the capital city of Patna with 10,93,642 members. PACS is the most prominent sector with 8,476 (31%) societies and having 1,36,29,113 members, followed by Dairy Sector having 7,662 societies with 5,68,474 members. As far as coverage of rural areas is concerned, it is seen that 21,618 societies are in rural areas while 5,022 societies are in urban areas. Most importantly, 100% Gram Panchayats have been covered with PACS. Cooperatives in Union Territory Chandigarh have played an integral role in advancing the socio-economic development of its residents. Operating under the provisions of the Punjab Cooperative Societies Act, 1961, and the Punjab Cooperative Societies Rules, 1963 (applicable to UT Chandigarh), the Registrar, Cooperative Societies, UT, Chandigarh, oversees the registration of diverse Cooperative Societies. As per the National Cooperative Database, a national level repository of data on cooperatives, Chandigarh comprises 476 Primary Cooperative Societies, with 196 currently operational, 221 non-functional, and 59 undergoing liquidations. All the Cooperative Societies are situated in urban areas. Across all the functional sectors, there are 49,721 members, wherein the Housing and Cooperative holds the highest number of societies (48.5%), with 19,075 members, followed by the Credit and Thrift Society (29.6%) with 14,454 members. Other notable cooperative sectors in UT Chandigarh include Agro-Processing/ Industrial Cooperative (5.2%), Labour Cooperatives (4.8%), and Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (3.6%).
