text: Monthly Activities Report of September from UT Ladakh Criteria Details Sector PACS/Horticulture/Agriculture Development/Cooperative development etc. Location Kharul, Kargil, UT Ladakh. Event/Activity Name Exhibition-cum-Stall Workshop organized by Fruit Growers’ Cooperative Societies under the banner of the International Year of Cooperatives (IYC) 2025. Brief Information on the Activity To commemorate the International Year of Cooperatives (IYC) 2025, the Fruit Growers’ Cooperative Societies held an exhibition-cum-stall workshop in Kharul, Kargil. In the previous month, the Hon'ble Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh formally opened the fruit farmers' stall complex, where the ceremony was conducted. Along with technical discussions and demonstrations on contemporary production, post-harvest management, and cooperative-based marketing tactics, the program featured locally grown fruits and value-added horticulture goods. Local farmers, cooperative members, local residents and agricultural specialists actively participated in the workshop, which offered an atmosphere for networking and knowledge sharing. Objective  To celebrate the 2025 International Year of Cooperatives and advance cooperative development in agriculture.  To improve farmers' knowledge of scientific fruit marketing, processing, and farming.  To encourage value addition and fortify cooperative networks in order to improve livelihoods sustainably.  To promote women's and youth involvement in the cooperative sector in order to promote inclusive rural development. No. of Participants 55 Achievements & Outcomes  Greater knowledge of contemporary horticultural techniques and the advantages of cooperation among fruit growers.  Improved connections between local farmers, government organizations, and cooperatives.  Increasing market exposure for local horticultural industry through the effective display of regional fruit varieties and processed goods.  The recently constructed stall complex became known as a center for Kargil's cooperative-led horticultural growth.  Increased participation in cooperative activities by women and youth. Photographs & AV Content Additional Remarks PHOTO GALLERY Criteria Details Sector PACS/Women Empowerment/Handloom/Handicrafts/ Cooperative Development etc. Location Tourist Felicitation Centre (TFC), Kargil District, UT Ladakh. Event/Activity Name Participation of Khawos Women Cooperative Society Limited in National Handloom Day 2025 - Exhibition and Craft Mela under IYC 2025. Brief Information on the Activity At TFC Kargil, the Handloom and Handicraft Department commemorated National Handloom Day 2025. Local artists' products were on display at a Craft Mela. Khawos Women Cooperative Society Limited took part by showcasing traditional shawls, carpets, and woolen clothes, encouraging women's cooperative growth and entrepreneurship under IYC 2025. Objective  Encourage economic empowerment and cooperatives run by women.  To provide marketing and to promote traditional handicrafts and handloom items.  Give local women craftsmen access to markets.  Inform people about cooperative values and IYC 2025.  Encourage women and young people to join cooperatives. No. of Participants 340 Achievements & Outcomes  Increased Khawos Women Cooperative Society sales and visibility.  Increased knowledge of cooperative enterprise and women's cooperatives.  Created an opportunity for market connections and networking.  Promoted the handicraft and cultural heritage of Ladakh. Photographs & AV Content Additional Remarks PHOTO GALLERY Criteria Details Sector PACS/Dairy/Fisheries/Cooperative development etc. Location Khaltse, Leh, UT Ladakh. Event/Activity Name Awareness Camp cum Workshop on the Celebration of International Year of Cooperatives (IYC) 2025 Brief Information on the Activity The International Year of Cooperatives (IYC) 2025 was celebrated in Khaltse, Leh, with an Awareness Camp/Workshop. The purpose of the workshop was to inform the local community about the opportunities, advantages, and guiding principles of cooperatives. Cooperative management, financial literacy, and cooperative entrepreneurship were explained through interactive sessions. The workshop was aimed at fostering a cooperative culture in the area, and active participation was seen from the local stakeholders, young people, and cooperative members. Objective  Educate local communities about the 2025 International Year of Cooperatives (IYC).  Educate participants about the contribution cooperatives make to social and economic advancement.  Encourage women and young people to be self- sufficient and to engage in cooperative business.  Enhance understanding of best practices, financial literacy, and cooperative governance.  Promote networking and community involvement in collaborative projects. No. of Participants 65 Achievements & Outcomes  The local community is now more aware of the various cooperative schemes and its advantages.  Encouraged women and young people to participate in cooperative activities.  Improved connections between cooperative organizations and the community.  Encouraged the cooperative movement as a means of achieving sustainable local growth. Photographs & AV Content Additional Remarks PHOTO GALLERY Criteria Details Sector PACS/Dairy/Fisheries/Agro-Processing/Cooperative Development etc. Location Fruits Growers Marketing and Processing Societies Ltd., Kargil, Ladakh. Event/Activity Name Sahkar Vaarta 2025 – Awareness and Performance Review under IYC 2025. Brief Information on the Activity Under the banner of the International Year of Cooperatives (IYC) 2025, the Sahkar Vaarta took place at the Fruits Growers Marketing and Processing Societies Ltd., Kargil, during the third week of September 2025. The event demonstrated how well local societies performed in putting various plans into action. At the event, students from the Government Girls Higher Secondary School in Kargil learned about fruit processing methods, such as how to make pulp, jam, juice, and dry apricots. Students gained an understanding of cooperative initiatives and value addition in horticulture through interactive demonstrations. Objective  Examine and highlight the local fruit producers' societies' scheme implementation performance.  Teach school children about agro-processing and cooperative based on horticulture products.  Raise awareness on importance of the International Year of Cooperatives (IYC 2025).  Showcase methods for adding value to fruits including local fruits like dry apricots, pulp, juice.  Encourage young people to get involved in entrepreneurship in field of agro-processing and cooperative activities. No. of Participants 55 Achievements & Outcomes  Greater knowledge of agro-processing methods and cooperative functioning among school children.  Highlighted the accomplishments and performance of local fruit producers' groups under variety of programs.  Promoted youth participation in cooperative-based entrepreneurship and gardening.  Displayed useful value-adding strategies, encouraging interest in a career in agro-processing.  Enhanced awareness of the cooperative movement's contribution to independence and regional prosperity. Photographs & AV Content Additional Remarks PHOTO GALLERY Criteria Details Sector PACS/Dairy/Fisheries/Cooperation development etc. Location Zanskar, Kargil District, UT Ladakh Event/Activity Name Participation of The Diary Cooperative Society in Ladakh Zanskar Festival 2025 under IYC 2025. Brief Information on the Activity Under the International Year of Cooperatives (IYC 2025) banner, the Diary Cooperative Society Atting set up a stall during the Ladakh Zanskar Festival 2025. The group displayed variety of dairy products made by its members, such as cheese, yogurt, milk, and other goods with added value. Visitors had the chance to learn about the cooperative activities, goods, and the advantages dairy cooperatives offer to regional economies, at the stall. Objective  Promote The Diary Cooperative Society's initiatives and its various products.  Educate people about the advantages of dairy cooperatives in light of IYC 2025.  Promote local involvement in collaborative projects.  Emphasize the methods used in dairy production for value addition and processing.  Encourage networking and community involvement with stakeholders and customers. No. of Participants 250 Achievements & Outcomes  Increased awareness and familiarity with The Diary Cooperative Society and its products and services.  Encouraged cooperative entrepreneurship and value addition based on dairy.  Increased knowledge among festival goers of the cooperative model.  Improved connections between customers, society, and other cooperative stakeholders.  Stimulated interest in and involvement in regional cooperative and dairy projects. Photographs & AV Content Additional Remarks PHOTO GALLERY

text: Government of Tamil Nadu Department of Cooperation – September 2025 Activity Report – International Year of Cooperatives 2025 Criteria Details Sector All Level State Event/Activity Name Power of Cooperatives in transformation of Economy – Exposure Visits Brief Information on the Activity The programme on “Power of Cooperatives in Transformation of Economy” is designed to showcase how cooperative movements have become key drivers of inclusive growth, rural development, and economic resilience in the modern era. Cooperatives today are not only limited to traditional sectors like agriculture, credit, and dairy but are also emerging as significant players in new -age domains such as digital platforms, renewable energy, value addition, and export promotion. As part of this initiative, exposure visits to successful cooperative enterprises in neighbouring states was organised. These visits focused on the following activities:  Field visits to leading cooperatives in sectors such as dairy, banking, agro -processing, marketing, fisheries, handlooms, and consumer retail.  Interactive sessions and knowledge sharing with cooperative leaders, managers, and policymakers to understand governance models, business strategies, and innovation practices.  Workshops and group discussions on cooperative policies, legal frameworks, digital transformation, and sustainability models.  Documentation and experience sharing sessions post- visit to develop actionable strategies for replication and scaling of best practices in home institutions. Objective  To enhance the understanding of cooperative members on the evolving role of cooperatives in socio-economic development.  To study successful cooperative models and best practices from other states and adopt them in local contexts.  To build leadership, managerial, and entrepreneurial capacities among cooperative members through practical exposure.  To promote innovation, diversification, and sustainability in cooperative activities by learning from field -level experiences.  To strengthen inter -state collaboration and knowledge exchange among cooperative institutions No. of Participants 500 from all districts of Tamil Nadu Achievements & Outcomes  Enhanced awareness among cooperative members on the strategic role of cooperatives in transforming the local and national economy.  Adoption of innovative management practices and diversification strategies based on exposure experiences.  Development of actionable plans for strengthening cooperative governance, member participation, and financial sustainability.  Strengthened networks and partnerships between cooperatives across states for knowledge exchange an d collaborative initiatives.  Empowered cooperative leaders capable of steering their societies towards growth, competitiveness, and social impact in the modern economic landscape. Exposure Trip to Hyderabad, inaugurated by Additional Registrar (MD, TNCU) Additional Registrar (Consumer Activities) and Additional Registrar (Budget & Planning) from the RCS Office. Press release on Cooperative members exposure trip Cooperative Society Members Exposure Trip to Kerala Cooperative members visited Balaramapuram Cooperative Society, Kerala - Field exposure trip on operations of the handloom production. Sales outlet for handicraft products made by the members of Kerala Arts & Crafts village, which is being operated through Urulungal Contract Workers Cooperative Society was explained to the members. The modern agricultural area known as KASCO village spread over 30 acres under the Karakulam Service Cooperative Society (KASCO), was visited by the members. They were shown the agricultural lands, fish ponds, goat and cattle rearing units and the members were given an explanation of their participation and contribution to the society. An explanation of the operations of the Green Dew coconut oil production center, run by the Nanniyodu Cooperative Society, was given to the members. An explanation of the operations of the Green Dew coconut oil production center, run by the Nanniyodu Cooperative Society, was given to the members.

title: CFC%2C%20Sironcha_0.pdf
text: DDM, Gadchiroli Conducted of Cooperative Literacy Camp at Sironcha As advised by RO, we conducted a Cooperative Literacy Camp at Sironcha blocks for district functionaries, cooperative department, APMC, Cooperative Marketing Societies and non - ooperative societies, etc. on 1 7 September 2025. The programme was inaugurated by Shri Shree N Bhandariwar, Vice -President, GDCCB, Shri C M Totawa, Development Officer, Shri N V Paunikar, DDM, Shri P D Uike, DGM, Aheri RO, Shri C G Mukkawar, BN, Sironcha branch, and 70 participants from Fisheries societies. The main objective of the program was to provide information on initiatives taken by MoC and NABARD on the Cooperatives sector, various schemes for PACS/dairy/Fisheries societies. The object of International Coop erative Year is to provide goods and services to the consumers at a reasonable cost with the aim to encourage them towards productivity, savings, investments and equal distribution of surplus. The DDM, NABARD expressed their view on Cooperative years. Th e DDM said that the 7 principal of cooperatives are Voluntary and Open Membership, Democratic Member Control, Members' Economic Participation, Autonomy and Independence, Education, Training, and Information, Cooperation among Cooperatives, and Concern for Community. These principles serve as guidelines for cooperatives to operate effectively by ensuring democratic control, member involvement, and a commitment to the well-being of their members and the broader community. the Ministry of Cooperative has tak en various initiative for improve status of cooperative sectors like model bye -laws for PACS making them multipurpose, multidimensional and transparent entities, Strengthening of PACS through computerization, new multipurpose PACS/Dairy/Fisheries Cooperatives in uncovered panchayats, world’s Largent decentralized grain storage plan in cooperative sector to ensure food security, PACS as common Service Centre for better access to e-service, formation of new FPO by PACS, PACS given priority for Retail Petrol/diesel outlets, PACS eligible for LPG distributorship for diversifying its activities, PACS as Jan Aushadhi Kendra for improving access to generic medicines at rural level, PACS as Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samriddhi Kendras for fertilizer distribution, converge nce of PM - KUSUM at PACS level for energy security, etc. The Ministry has provided relief to cooperative societies in Income Tax Act, like surcharge reduced from 12% to 7% for cooperative societies having income between Rs.1 to 10 crore, MAT reduced for cooperative from 18.5% to 15%, a clarification has been issued to remove difficulties in cash transactions by cooperatives under Section 269ST of IT Act. etc. NABARD initiatives has taken various initiatives for improve status of cooperative sectors like Institutional Development, Financial Inclusion and Banking Technology, Skilling and Marketing for Rural SHGs and POs and Refinance Support to DCCB, etc. Shri C M Totawar, Development Officer had expressed their view on Crop loan, loan to SHG members and PMFBY. He said that all banks of the district is interested to disburse crop loan to all eligible farmers. Farmers should visit their nearby bank branches and submit the required documents to Branch Manager for crop loan. He said that the primary objective of a Self-Help Group (SHG) is to empower its members by providing a platform for financial inclusion, fostering entrepreneurship, and promoting social and economic development. SHGs achieve this through regular savings, access to microfinance, and collective action to address common challenges. He said that the aim to enhance the skills and capabilities of members through training, capacity-building programs, and knowledge sharing. Self-help groups foster social cohesion by creating a sense of community , promoting mutual support, and encouraging collective decision-making. The programme ended with a vote of thanks. (N V Paunikar) Manager

The DDM said that the 7 principal of cooperatives are Voluntary and Open Membership, Democratic Member Control, Members' Economic Participation, Autonom y and Independence, Education, Training, and Information, Cooperation among Cooperatives, and Concern for Community. These principles serve as guidelines for cooperatives to operate effectively by ensuring democratic control, member involvement, and a commitment to the well-being of their members and the broader community. the Ministry of Cooperative has taken various initiative for improve status of cooperative sectors like model bye -laws for PACS making them multipurpose, multidimensional and transparent entities, Strengthening of PACS through computerization, new multipurpose PACS/Dairy/Fisheries Cooperatives in uncovered panchayats, world’s Largent decentralized grain storage plan in cooperative sector to ensure food security, PACS as common Service Centre for better access to e-service, formation of new FPO by PACS, PACS given priority for Retail Petrol/diesel outlets, PACS eligible for LPG distributorship for diversifying its activities, PACS as Jan Aushadhi Kendra for improving access to generic medicines at rural level, PACS as Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samriddhi Kendras for fertilizer distribution, convergence of PM - KUSUM at PACS level for energy security, etc. The Ministry has provided relief to cooperative societies in Income Tax Act, like surcharge reduced from 12% to 7% for cooperative societies having income between Rs.1 to 10 crore, MAT reduced for cooperative from 18.5% to 15%, a clarification has been issued to remove difficulties in cash transactions by cooperatives under Section 269ST of IT Act. etc. NABARD initiatives has taken various initiatives for improve status of cooperative sectors like Institutional Development, Financial Inclusion and Banking Technology, Skilling and Marketing for Rural SHGs and POs and Refinance Support to DCCB, etc. Shri Raju Sorte, GM, GDCCB had expressed their view on Crop loan, loan to SHG members and PMFBY. He said that all banks of the district is interested to disburse crop loan to all eligible farmers. Farmers should visit their nearby bank branches and s ubmit the required documents to Branch Manager for crop loan. He said that the primary objective of a Self-Help Group (SHG) is to empower its members by providing a platform for financial inclusion, fostering entrepreneurship, and promoting social and economic development. SHGs achieve this through regular savings, access to microfinance, and collective action to address common challenges. He said that the aim to enhance the skills and capabilities of members through training, capacity-building programs, and knowledge sharing. Self -help groups foster social cohesion by creating a sense of community, promoting mutual support, and encouraging collective decision-making. The programme ended with a vote of thanks. (N V Paunikar) Manager

text: No. L-1 20131212021-l&P Government of lndia Ministry "::"oeration Krishi Bhawan, New Delhi Dated: 3oth June, 2022 ORDER Sub: Constitution of National Level Monitoring and lmplementation Gommittee (NLMIC) for the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerization of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)-reg. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), in its meeting held on 29th June, 2022, has approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerization of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS). In this regard, the approval of Competent Authority is conveyed for constitution of the National Level Monitoring and lmplementation Committee (NLMIC) as under:- 1) Secretary (M/o Cooperation, Go!) (Chairman) 2) Additional Secretary & Financial Advisor (M/o Cooperation, Gol) 3) Joint Secretary (M/o Cooperation, Gol) 4) Chairman, NABARD 5) Principal Secretaries (Cooperation) of selected States. 6) Representative of NlTl Aayog 7) CEOs of selected State Cooperative Banks. 8) Deputy Managing Director (lDD), NABARD - Member Secretary The project details document is attached herewith for ready reference.2 Encl. PSO to Joint Secretary (CTP/!T) I Government of lndia Ministry of Cooperation New Delhi, 30thJun e,2022 Proiect Details Computerisation of PACS 1. INTRODUCTION 1.1 The agri-rural landscape of the country is predominantly serviced by the three tier Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) for the financial and non- financial needs of the farmers, especially the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs). The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) are playing vital role in developing socio- economic conditions of the cooperatives and are the first stage which is formed by individual farmers. The 2nd tier is known as District Central Cooperative Bank which provides direct linkages to the PACS through the direct financing of primary societies. The 3'd tier at the apex level is the State Cooperative Bank which control and coordinate the finances of District Central Cooperative Banks. 1.2 This structure consist of a network of about 95,000 Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), 351 District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBS) and 33 State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). As per the preliminary information given by NABARD, out of these 95,000 PACS, about 63,000 are functiona!. The important criteria for considering a PACS to be functional is updating & auditing of annual accounts annually and providing credit or non-credit services to its members. 1.3 National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD),has taken the initiative to bring most of the State and District Central Cooperative Banks on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) have so far been out of the ambit of any such technology support. 1 .4 The proposed project envisages computerization of the activities undertaken by the PACS mainly focusing on crediUnon-credit business related to Agriculture and Allied activities. The key components of the project are Hardware, comprehensive Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) solution, Project Monitoring Unit (PMU), Training, Handholding support and Maintenance etc. ln North East and Tribal Areas of the country, due to thinly populated area, Large Sized Adivasi Multi-Purpose Co-operative Page 1 of I Government of India Ministry of Cooperation Societies (LAMPS) are prevalent which function more or less similar to PACS. Such LAMPS or any other farmers service society similar to PACS will also be covered in this project within the proposed budget outlay. 2. IMPLEMENTATION METHODOLOGY 2.1The project envisages use of one common software across the country to capture data on all functionalities of PACS, both credit and non-credit. The project software will run on online mode and internet connectivity is to be provided by the State Governments, who may utilise the services of BHARAT Net project of Ministry of Communications for this purpose. 2.2 Basic Architecture of the Project 2.2.1 At the National Level, NABARD will engage a vendor namely National Level PACS Software Vendor (NLPSV) to provide the common software including cyber security and data storage through open bidding as per the provisions of General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017. At the State level, NABARD will prepare and publish a central panel of System lntegrators (Sls) through open bidding. States are to select the Sls from this central panel with a ceiling on number of PACS that one Sl can take up. Sls will supply hardware, prepare legacy data, digitise and port this data into software, recommend state specific customization required in the common software and provide the support system. 2.2.2 ln the project, there will also be a provision to run the software on offline mode and later upload the data in the system in case of network issue. Data would be either routed through the DCCBs or State Data Centres to the Central Core Data Centre/National Level Data Repository (NLDR). NLDR will be hosted on cloud storage. 2.2.3 PACS in some States are at different levels of computerization. lt means some PACS have been computerised (mostly working on a stand-alone basis) and others not computerised at all. ln respect of PACS which have been computerised, expenditure will be reimbursed to States @ { 50,000/- per PACS subject to the condition that, (i) they integrate their software with the Central Common Software, (ia) their hardware Page 2 of 8 Government of lndia Ministry of Cooperation meets the required specifications, and (iii) the computerization of PACS was commissioned by the State on or after 1st February,2017 i.e. the date of 2017-18 budget announcement. PACS which have not been computerised by such states will also be taken up under this project at full cost. 2.2.4 Functional PACS will be selected by the State Governments for Computerization as per priority mentioned in para 5.1. A re-survey is being done by NABARD and due prioritisation of PACS would be done for taking up in the project. 2.2.5 For sustainability of the project, maintenance and handholding of the software and hardware is considered critical. For this purpose, the Project envisages a support system by setting up one support centre on an average at cluster of every 200 PACS. These support centres will report to State PMUs which will also serve as State level support centre. This entire support system will be under the overall supervision and contro! of the State Govt. These support centres will be set up and operated by the concerned Sl. 2.2.6 After migration to the software, employee (s) of the PACS will be given adequate training about functioning of the software and how to work on it. Hands on training will be given through National Council for Cooperative Training (NCCT) institutions and Scheme of Financial Assistance for Training of Cooperative Banks Personnel (SOFTCOB) assisted lnstitutions like Agricultural Cooperative Staff Training lnstitutes (ACSTIs) and other Cooperative Training lnstitutes under the administrative contro! of State Govt. 2.2.7 For implementation and monitoring of the project, creation of a core team at NABARD, Head Office with the team members constituted from its officers has been envisaged. This core team will be assisted by Project Monitoring Unit (PMU) hired by NABARD for the project. NABARD may hire people/professional/technical experts for the PMU on contractual basis. Similarly, NABARD will set up state PMUs to assist States in implementation and monitoring of the project at state level which will also function as the state level support centres. These State PMUs will also be manned by NABARD officials and contractual staff. Page 3 of 8 Government of lndia Ministry of Cooperation 3. ROLES & RESPONSIBILITIES of various stakeholders and implementation and monitoring framework of the project 3.1 Government of lndia:- Government of lndia i.e. Ministry of Cooperation will be responsible for the overall implementation and monitoring of the project through National level Monitoring and implementation Committee to ensure real-time monitoring and effective feed-back about the implementation of the proposed project to be set up as under:- (i) National level Monitoring and lmplementation Committee(NLMIC) comprising of a) b) c) d) e) 0 s) h) Secretary (M/o Cooperation, Gol) (Chairman) Additional Secretary & Financial Advisor (M/o Cooperation, Gol) Joint Secretary (M/o Cooperation, Gol) Chairman, NABARD Principal Secretary (Coop)-State Government (s)- Five States by rotation (will be rotated every year). Representative of NlTl Aayog CEOs of five State Cooperative Banks (by rotation) Deputy Managing Director (lDD), NABARD -Member Secretary Role of NLMIC:- * guide and steer the implementation of the project. n approve the guidelines for implementation of the project. * review the progress of implementation of the project periodically * to consider and authorize the appropriation of the funds from one component of the project to another within the overall budget outlay of the project, if required. * Monitor functioning of central PMU 3.2 State Governments/STCBS/DCCBS:-State Governments will be responsible for implementation and monitoring of the project in their respective states. Also, evaluation and recommendation of the proposals to be fonruarded to NABARD for approva! through State level lmplementation and Monitoring Committee to be set up as follows:- 3.2.1 State level lmplementation & Monitoring Committee (SLlMG)comprising of Page 4 of 8 a) b) c) d) e) 0 Government of lndia Ministry of Cooperation Add l. Ch ief Secretary/Principal Secretary, Co-operation- Chairperson Principal Secretary/Secretary (Finance) Registrar of Cooperative Societies (RCS) Chief General Manager (CGM), NABARD Three identified DCCBs (by rotation) in three tier Structure MD/CEO-State Cooperative Bank - Member Secretary Role of State Leve! Implementation & Monitoring Committee * to implement the approved guidelines at the state level and provide feedback to NLMIC. * to guide and steer the implementation of the project in the state. * To examine and recommend the proposals to be taken up in this project. 3.2.2 District Level Implementation & Monitoring Committee comprising District Development Manager (DDM), NABARD and officials notified by the respective State/UT Governments under the Chairmanship of District Collector/District Magistrate. MD, District Cooperative Bank will be the member convener. There will be representation of selected PACS at the level of District Level Committees. Role of District Level lmplementation & Monitoring Committee * To be the first line of implementation and monitoring system within the overall framework. * lt will be responsible for the smooth implementation of the project as per approved guidelines and provide necessary support like power, connectivity, etc. 3.3 NABARD:-NABARD will be responsible for implementation of the project at Central level under the guidance and directions of National Level Monitoring and lmplementation Committee and Ministry of Cooperation. lt will establish a core team of its officers of this purpose which will be assisted by a Project Monitoring Unit (PMU) manned by professionals and experts. Further, NABARD will also act as a custodian on behalf of Go! of the common software and all the financial and personal data generated/captured on the software. After completion of the project, NABARD will manage the system in coordination with the State Governments and will be responsible for its sustainability. Page 5 of 8 Government of lndia Ministry of Cooperation 3.3.1 Project Monitoring Unit (PMU) at Central level will: - * Be set up by NABARD and manned by Management & Technical Experts. * Finalize project design and implementation strategy. * Stakeholder consultation with States, Central govt. RBl, Banks etc. * Finalize the requirement of hardware and functionalities of software for the project. * Bidding and short Iisting exercise as per the provisions of General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017. * Provide technical support during and after the implementation of the proposed Project. {. Guide the NLPSV regarding customization of the central software based on the state-wise feedbacUneeds. * Provide guidance to the state level PMUs. * Provide necessary inputs to the National level Monitoring and lmplementing Committee (NLMIC). * Prepare necessary reports and dashboards (MlS etc.) for facilitating review at National/State Level. * Periodical reporting of the progress to the Government of lndia. * Provide guidance on the business aspects to the PACS as well as monitor the implementation carried out by the selected vendors. * Planning and execution of the training and capacity building at all levels. * Ensure the preservation of the data and provide measures for data analysis & analytics. * Undertake all other matters necessary for the successful implementation of the project duly consulting NABARD/GoI. 3.3.2 Project Monitoring Units (PMUs) at the State Ievel will: - * Be manned by NABARD's officials and Management & Technical Experts. * Will function under the overall guidance of the Central PMU and report to State Secretary of Co-operation Department. Page 6 of 8 Government of India Ministry of Cooperation * Provide managemenUtechnical support during and after the implementation of the proposed Project. * ldentification of functional PACS for computerization in consultation of State Government within overall project guidelines. * Responsible for identifying the customization needs at the state level and report to the central PMU/SI. * Liaise with state level stakeholders. * Arranging for stakeholder capacity building at the state level. * Follow up for successful implementation at the state level. * Provide guidance on the business aspects to the PACS as well as monitor the implementation carried out by the selected vendors. {. Prepare necessary reports (MlS etc.) for facilitating review at State Level. * Facilitate planning and successful execution of the training and capacity building at all State/PACS level as advised by Central PMU. * Undertake all other matters necessary for the successful implementation of the project duly consulting all the stakeholders. 4. PROJECT COST & FUNDING PATTERN 4.1 The project of Computerization of PACS will be taken up at a total cost of { 2516 crore and per PACS cost of { 3.91 lakhs (approx.). The overall share of Government of lndia (Gol) would be t 1528 crore, State Government would be t 736 crore and NABARD is < 252 crore. 4.2 Cost sharing pattern for General States and North Eastern/ Himalayan States will be in the ratio as indicated below: 4.2.1 Comprehensive Software (including Cyber Security & Data Storage) and Training:- Cost of this component will be shared by Gol and NABARD. NABARD will contribute Rs. 252 cr. and the rest wil! be borne by Gol. Page 7 of 8 Government of lndia Ministry of Cooperation .4.2.2 Other Components (Hardware, Digitization & Support system) :- Share of Gol:State will be in 60:40 ratio. For North Eastern and Hilly States, it will be 90:10. For UTs (without legislature) 1 00% cost will be borne by Gol. For UTs with legislature, it will be 80:20. 4.2.3 PMU and Administrative Cost:- Expenditure on both Centre and State PMUs and project administration will be borne by Gol up to { 50 cr. Any cost in excess of this will be met by NABARD from its own resources. Salary of regular officers of NABARD would not be charged to the project cost. 4.3 For software, training cost and PMU cost, share of Gol will be transferred to NABARD as per the payment timelines of the contract with the National Level PACS Software Vendor (NLPSV), contractors providing manpower for PMUs and training schedules. As regards other components, Gol share will be transferred to States. 5. TIME LINES 5.1 PACS with no computerization will be prioritized, followed by PACS with computerization but may need up-gradation. PACS which have already been computerized through State Govt./StCBs/DCCBs intervention would be considered in the last. Year-wise phasing of the project is given in Table 1 : Table 1 Year Total No of PACS to be computerized Maintenance and hand- holding support Year I 2022-23 13,000 Handholding support of total 5 years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. Year ll 2023-24 20,000 Year lll 2024-25 30,000 Year IV 2025-26 Year V 2026-27 Total 63,000 5.2 Sunset date of the project will be 31 .03.2027 Page 8 of 8

Also, evaluation and recommendation of the proposals to be fonruarded to NABARD for approva! through State level lmplementation and Monitoring Committee to be set up as follows:- 3.2.1 State level lmplementation & Monitoring Committee (SLlMG)comprising of Page 4 of 8 a) b) c) d) e) 0 Government of lndia Ministry of Cooperation Add l. Ch ief Secretary/Principal Secretary, Co-operation- Chairperson Principal Secretary/Secretary (Finance) Registrar of Cooperative Societies (RCS) Chief General Manager (CGM), NABARD Three identified DCCBs (by rotation) in three tier Structure MD/CEO-State Cooperative Bank - Member Secretary Role of State Leve! Implementation & Monitoring Committee * to implement the approved guidelines at the state level and provide feedback to NLMIC. * to guide and steer the implementation of the project in the state. * To examine and recommend the proposals to be taken up in this project. 3.2.2 District Level Implementation & Monitoring Committee comprising District Development Manager (DDM), NABARD and officials notified by the respective State/UT Governments under the Chairmanship of District Collector/District Magistrate. MD, District Cooperative Bank will be the member convener. There will be representation of selected PACS at the level of District Level Committees. Role of District Level lmplementation & Monitoring Committee * To be the first line of implementation and monitoring system within the overall framework. * lt will be responsible for the smooth implementation of the project as per approved guidelines and provide necessary support like power, connectivity, etc. 3.3 NABARD:-NABARD will be responsible for implementation of the project at Central level under the guidance and directions of National Level Monitoring and lmplementation Committee and Ministry of Cooperation. lt will establish a core team of its officers of this purpose which will be assisted by a Project Monitoring Unit (PMU) manned by professionals and experts. Further, NABARD will also act as a custodian on behalf of Go! of the common software and all the financial and personal data generated/captured on the software. After completion of the project, NABARD will manage the system in coordination with the State Governments and will be responsible for its sustainability. RBl, Banks etc. * Finalize the requirement of hardware and functionalities of software for the project. * Bidding and short Iisting exercise as per the provisions of General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017. * Provide technical support during and after the implementation of the proposed Project. {. Guide the NLPSV regarding customization of the central software based on the state-wise feedbacUneeds. * Provide guidance to the state level PMUs. * Provide necessary inputs to the National level Monitoring and lmplementing Committee (NLMIC). * Prepare necessary reports and dashboards (MlS etc.) for facilitating review at National/State Level. * Periodical reporting of the progress to the Government of lndia. * Provide guidance on the business aspects to the PACS as well as monitor the implementation carried out by the selected vendors. * Planning and execution of the training and capacity building at all levels. * Ensure the preservation of the data and provide measures for data analysis & analytics. * Undertake all other matters necessary for the successful implementation of the project duly consulting NABARD/GoI. 3.3.2 Project Monitoring Units (PMUs) at the State Ievel will: - * Be manned by NABARD's officials and Management & Technical Experts. * Will function under the overall guidance of the Central PMU and report to State Secretary of Co-operation Department. PROJECT COST & FUNDING PATTERN 4.1 The project of Computerization of PACS will be taken up at a total cost of { 2516 crore and per PACS cost of { 3.91 lakhs (approx.). The overall share of Government of lndia (Gol) would be t 1528 crore, State Government would be t 736 crore and NABARD is < 252 crore. 4.2 Cost sharing pattern for General States and North Eastern/ Himalayan States will be in the ratio as indicated below: 4.2.1 Comprehensive Software (including Cyber Security & Data Storage) and Training:- Cost of this component will be shared by Gol and NABARD. NABARD will contribute Rs. 252 cr. and the rest wil! be borne by Gol. For North Eastern and Hilly States, it will be 90:10. For UTs (without legislature) 1 00% cost will be borne by Gol. For UTs with legislature, it will be 80:20. 4.2.3 PMU and Administrative Cost:- Expenditure on both Centre and State PMUs and project administration will be borne by Gol up to { 50 cr. Any cost in excess of this will be met by NABARD from its own resources. Salary of regular officers of NABARD would not be charged to the project cost. 4.3 For software, training cost and PMU cost, share of Gol will be transferred to NABARD as per the payment timelines of the contract with the National Level PACS Software Vendor (NLPSV), contractors providing manpower for PMUs and training schedules. As regards other components, Gol share will be transferred to States. 5. TIME LINES 5.1 PACS with no computerization will be prioritized, followed by PACS with computerization but may need up-gradation. text: DDM, Gadchiroli Conducted of Cooperative Literacy Camp at Dhanora As advised by RO, we conducted a Cooperative Literacy Camp at Dhanora blocks for district functionaries, cooperative department, APMC, Cooperative Marketing Societies and non - cooperative societies, etc. on 16 September 2025. The programme was inaugurated b y Shri Anant Salve, Honorary Secretary, GDCCB, Dhanora, Shri Raju Sorte, GM, Loan Section, Shri N V Paunikar, DDM, Shri Mukesh Shanane, Branch Manager, Ananta Khadatkar, Inspector of GDCCB and 36 participants from various societies. The main objective of the program was to provide information on initiatives taken by MoC and NABARD on the Cooperatives sector, various schemes for PACS/dairy/Fisheries societies. The object of International Cooperative Year is to provide goods and services to the consumers at a reasonable cost with the aim to encourage them towards productivity, savings, investments and equal distribution of surplus. The DDM, NABARD expressed their view on Cooperative years. The DDM said that the 7 principal of cooperatives are Voluntary and Open Membership, Democratic Member Control, Members' Economic Participation, Autonomy and Independence, Education, Training, and Information, Cooperation among Cooperatives, and Concern for Community. These principles serve as guidelines for cooperatives t o operate effectively by ensuring democratic control, member involvement, and a commitment to the well-being of their members and the broader community. the Ministry of Cooperative has taken various initiative for improve status of cooperative sectors li ke model bye -laws for PACS making them multipurpose, multidimensional and transparent entities, Strengthening of PACS through computerization, new multipurpose PACS/Dairy/Fisheries Cooperatives in uncovered panchayats, world’s Largent decentralized grain storage plan in cooperative sector to ensure food security, PACS as common Service Centre for better access to e-service, formation of new FPO by PACS, PACS given priority for Retail Petrol/diesel outlets, PACS eligible for LPG distributorship for diversifying its activities, PACS as Jan Aushadhi Kendra for improving access to generic medicines at rural level, PACS as Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samriddhi Kendras for fertilizer distribution, convergence of PM - KUSUM at PACS level for energy security, etc. The Ministry has provided relief to cooperative societies in Income Tax Act, like surcharge reduced from 12% to 7% for cooperative societies having income between Rs.1 to 10 crore, MAT reduced for cooperative from 18.5% to 15%, a clarification has been issued to remove difficulties in cash transactions by cooperatives under Section 269ST of IT Act. etc. NABARD initiatives has taken various initiatives for improve status of cooperative sectors like Institutional Development, Financial Inclusion and Banking Technology, Skilling and Marketing for Rural SHGs and POs and Refinance Support to DCCB, etc. Shri Raju Sorte, GM, GDCCB had expressed their view on Crop loan, loan to SHG members and PMFBY. He said that all banks of the district is interested to disburse crop loan to all eligible farmers. Farmers should visit their nearby bank branches and submit the required documents to Branch Manager for crop loan. He said that the primary objective of a Self-Help Group (SHG) is to empower its members by providing a platfo rm for financial inclusion, fostering entrepreneurship, and promoting social and economic development. SHGs achieve this through regular savings, access to microfinance, and collective action to address common challenges. He said that the aim to enhance t he skills and capabilities of members through training, capacity-building programs, and knowledge sharing. Self -help groups foster social cohesion by creating a sense of community, promoting mutual support, and encouraging collective decision-making. The programme ended with a vote of thanks. (N V Paunikar) Manager

text: Internal INTER OFFICE MEMORANDUM Ref.No.NB.JH.DDM(Ramgarh)/491/IDD-CLC/2025-26 Date: 03 October 2025 ===================================================== For : CGM, NABARD, Jharkhand R.O., Ranchi From : DDM, NABARD, Ramgarh, Jharkhand ===================================================== Cooperative Literacy Camp for PACS officials at Patratu Block of Ramgarh district on 16.09.2025 - Back to Office Report Please find attached herewith the BTOR for Cooperative Literacy Camp for PACS officials at Patratu Block of Ramgarh district held on 16.09.2025 (Deepa Priyanka) DDM, Ramgarh Encl: as above Internal Back to Office Report (BTOR) Sr.No. Particulars Remarks 1 Name of the Project/Programme Cooperative Literacy Camp for PACS officials at Patratu Block 2 Place Bhurkunda Branch, Jharkhand State Cooperative Bank (JStCB), Patratu Block 3 Date 16.09.2025 4 Name of Organization/NGO/ Person visited DDM, Branch Manager (Bhurkunda branch, JStCB), JStCB officials, PACS officials, System Integrator (SI) Organised By NABARD in coordination with JStCB 5 Purpose of Visit To attend Cooperative Literacy Camp for PACS officials at Patratu Block 6 Topic Discussed The participants were introduced to the significance of celebrating the International Year of Cooperatives 2025. Detailed discussions were held on the Centrally Sponsored PACS Computerisation Project, which aims to make PACS more transparent, efficient and service-oriented. The role of PACS as Multi Service Centres (MSC) was emphasised, with examples of diversification into custom hiring, CSCs and agri-input outlets. The session also covered the World’s Largest Grain Storage Plan and its potential to create storage capacity at PACS level, KCC issuance through PACS, sanction of ST (others) limits for fertiliser and input business, and opportunities under AIF for infrastructure development. 7 Outcome of Visit – Action Points System Integrator (SI) Training & Handholding 1. SI to ensure mandatory 14 -day training and handholding support for PACS. Internal 2. Trainings must be made more effective and practical, with rigorous handholding at field level. Capacity Building of PACS Officials 1. Many PACS officials are still unable to perform voucher entry and day -end operations; some can only enter membership data. 2. SI to design refresher training modules focusing on critical functions. SI staff to assist PACS in: 1. Uploading legacy documents and registration certificates. 2. Entering asset details. PACS officials to be trained and engaged on document uploading and ERP operations to achieve target within timelines. Monitoring by JSTCB JSTCB officials advised to closely monitor the progress and ensure timely follow -up with SI and PACS. 8 Any other information, if any Internal Internal

text: Page 1 of 4 National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories Ltd. Monthly Activities Report – August, 2025 09/09/2025 Event: 1/3 Criteria Details Location Date: 02nd August, 2025 Venue: Pune Event/ Activity Name Presentation on India Vs. Brazil sugar sector market and policy scenario. Brief Information on the Activity With a view to visit prominent sugar & ethanol plants and meet prominent stakeholders including policy makers during Brazil’s peak operation period, NFCSF in association with Brazilian Embassy in Delhi and Indian Embassy in Brazil organized a ‘Brazil Study Visit’ under the leadership of Shri Harshvardhan Patil, President, NFCSF and was participated by Managing Director, NFCSF along with stalwarts of Indian Sugar & Allied Sector between 15-22 June, 2025. The 27 participants included one sitting Minister from Govt. of Maharashtra, One Member of Parliament, One Former Minister, Three MLAs, and Chairmen, Directors, technocrats, Engineers, Trader etc. The team visited various organizations and met industry leaders to understand their competitive advantages vis -à-vis Indian sugar market. These advantages ranges from policy support, technology adoption, sugarcane varietal advanatges etc. Based on this visit and knowledge acquired, Shri Prakash Naiknavare, MD, NFCSF delivered a presentation before the stalwarts of the Indian sugar industry at Pune, Maharashtra on 2nd August, 2025. Objective The objective was to help the participants understand the competitive ad vantage of the Brazilain sugar industry which is today the world’s largest sugar producer. No. of Participants 50 Achievements & Outcomes Participants were able to discuss the current situation of the Indian sugar industry and how to take it to the next phase of growth. The 2 hour discussion that followed reviewed major issues confronting the Indian sugar sector and the way forward plan Photographs & AV Content Attached Photographs & AV Content Additional Remarks Page 2 of 4 National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories Ltd. Monthly Activities Report – August, 2025 09/09/2025 Event: 2/3 Criteria Details Sector Sugar Location Date: 11th August, 2025 Venue: Pune Event / Activity Name Meeting with Ethiopian sugar delegation. Brief Information on the Activity NFCSF offers techno -commercial services to the domestic and international sugar industry towards establishment, expansion and modernization of sugar mills, ethanol plants and other bye - products. It is in this regard, a delegation of Ethiopian sugar industry met Shri Prakash Naiknavare, MD, NFCSF seeking guidance on expanding and modernizing their sugar industry. Objectives To provide techno-commercial guidance to the Ethiopian sugar industry. No. of Participants 10 Achievements & Outcomes The delegation explored the technical expertise and services that NFCSF can provide. Photographs & AV Contents Attached Additional Remarks Page 3 of 4 National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories Ltd. Monthly Activities Report – August, 2025 09/09/2025 Event: 3/3 Name of the Member: Karmyogi Ankushrao Tope Samarth Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana, Dist. Jalna (Maharashtra). Criteria Details Sector Sugar Location Date: 24th August, 2025 Venue: Jalna, Maharashtra Event / Activity Name Visit of Jt. Secretary, Ministry of Cooperation to Cooperative Sugar Mill. Brief Information on the Activity On 24 August, 2025, Mr D. K. Verma, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Cooperation. Govt of India visited Karmyogi Ankushrao Tope Samarth Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana, Dist. Jalna (Maharashtra). During the visit he inspected various projects of the Karkhana viz. sugar plant, Cogeneration plant, Etha nol plant. He also paid his tribute to the founder of the Karkhana at his memorial. He interacted with the Board of Directors of the Karkhana, during which he was inquisitive about actual functioning/activities of the cooperative sugar factory. He was cur ious to know the positive socioeconomic impact of the Karkhana on farmers. He took cognisance of the problems being faced by cooperative sugar industry put forth by the management & promised to look into the matters concerning the industry. He applauded the pioneering work done by the founder of the Karkhana, late Ankushrao Tope & also congratulated the present management ably led by Shri Rajesh Tope. Mr Verma also planted a sapling at the Karkhana administrative building under the campaign ’Ek ped maa ke naam’ launched by Hon PM. He also interacted with journalists present during his visit. The management & farmer members were left satisfied with the fruitful visit of a senior officer of Cooperation Ministry to experience the situation at ground level. title: International%20Year%20of%20Cooperative%2C%20Activity-Wise%20Report%20for%20Himachal%20Pradesh%20%28August%29.pdf
text: International Year of Cooperative: - Activities Wise Report in respect of Himachal Pradesh Criteria Details Sector PACS/ DCCB/StCB/Diary/Fisheries/Training Location All over Himachal Pradesh/In all AR Circles of Himachal Pradesh Event/Activity Name Awareness camp of Secretaries regarding computerization of PACS , Cooperative awareness program is organized for training and awareness generation among officials , Training program for nano urea sellers , Ek ped maa ke naam, Training Program for Fish Cooperative Societies in The Brahmanikalan Fish Cooperative Society Ltd Kosariyan Distt Bilaspur HP , Awareness & Training Session for Cooperative Members under HIMCOFED , Organization of CSC Training Programme , Independence Day Celebration & Flag Hosting, Cooperative Literacy Camp , Training program for fisheries cooperative societies, Workshop on Cooperative Business Model , Awareness Camp on (International Year of Cooperative)2025 , Agriculture, Horticulture and Swachhata me Sahakar Activities , Workshop on financial i ndependence through cooperative, Commencement of plantation drive under “Ek Ped Ma a ke Naam , National handloom Day , 07 -08-2025 celebration. Brief Information on the Activity  The 79th Independence Day was celebrated across various cooperative institutions in the State on 15th August 2025 with great enthusiasm under the banner of *International Cooperative Year 2025  The National Flag was hoisted, patriotic songs were sung, and workshops on financial independence through cooperatives were also organized.  Tree plantation drives were undertaken under the campaign “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam” by cooperative societies  Awareness camp and training programme on strengthening cooperative values, capacity building, and promoting sustainable cooperative business practices ,computerization of PACS is organized at society level  CSC Training Programme was conducted.  Awareness camps organized regarding training session Agriculture & Horticulture and Departmental Activities  Training programme was organized in collaboration with the Fisheries Department, participants were sensitized about Government initiatives in the fisheries sector.  HIMCOFED organized training and awareness programmes at the society level on tree plantation, fisheries, cooperative values, capacity building, and sustainable practices.  The 11th National Handloom Day was celebrated on 07th August 2025 at Bhuttico, Bhuthi Colony, Kullu. Objective  Awareness, education and information regarding cooperative movement.  Awareness, education and information regarding IFFCO fertilizer distribution.  To motivate Fishermen for Business Development , raise awareness about New Techniques in fisheries to raise their income resources  To create awareness about the contribution of cooperatives in India’s independence & development  To encourage youth participation in cooperative movement  To promote environmental consciousness and encourage individuals to contribute to ecological restoration by planting trees in memory/honor of their mothers.  To create awareness and build capacity at the grassroots level regarding the various services available through CSCs and how cooperatives can leverage them.  To build capacity of cooperative members under HIMCOFED  To create awareness on cooperative laws, rules, and financial discipline  To promote cooperative marketing and business opportunities  To strengthen members’ participation in cooperative governance  The objective of training given to secretaries about Common Service Centers (CSCs) is to ensure they understand the purpose, functions, and ope rations of CSCs so they can effectively facilitate public service delivery at the grassroots level.  To instill a sense of patriotism, unity, and national pride among members, staff, and the local community by celebrating India’s Independence Day through a respectful and meaningful flag hoisting ceremony, while also recognizing the role of cooperative institutions like PACS in the nation’s rural and agricultural development.  The importance of cooperative their role in rural up liftment.  Awareness about various welfare schemes and NABARD. Number of Participants 1033 Achievements & Outcomes  Increased sense of patriotism among participants ; Strengthened community bonding through cooperatives & awareness on cooperative values linked with national development  Improved understanding of cooperative principles and their practical application - Members motivated towards financial discipline and transparency - Awareness on latest schemes and government support for cooperatives  Over view of centrally sponsored Schemes.  Participants got insights into how Cooperative enterprises foster inclusivity, empower members and ensure long term social and economic benefits.  Trees have been pla nted and surroundings of cooperative societies are cleaned and members are made aware their rights about cooperatives.  Promotion of handloom products and encouragement of Artisans Photographs & AV Control Photos have been attached separately Additional Remarks All Societies have been directed by field functionaries during IYC meetings to perform the different activities to celebrate the year of cooperative a s per calendar circulated. All the field functionaries and staff have been directed to celebrate/organize month wise different activities as per IYC calendar plan already circulated. International Year of Cooperatives Activity-Wise Report for Himachal Pradesh (August) Thank You

text: ANNEXURE-A Scheme for distribution of Efficiency Awards for the year 2023-24 1. Only those factories who have submitted application in the prescribed format will be considered eligible for participation. 2. The cooperative sugar factories, which are having any dues to NFCSF, will not be considered for awards. The applications shall be accompanied with ‘No Dues Certificate' obtained from NFCSF. 3. The factories have been categorized in two zones namely (a) High Recovery Area (HRA) having Sugar recovery 10% and abo ve and (b) Other Recovery Area (ORA) i.e. recovery below 10%. The States falling under these two categories are as under:- a. High Recovery Area (HRA) - South Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka. [Note: South Gujarat comprises districts of Surat, Valsad, Bh aruch and Narmada in Gujarat State]. b. Other Recovery Area (ORA) - Areas other than those specified at (a) above. 4. If the actual installed capacity of the sugar mill is more than the licensed capacity, the actual installed capacity shall be reckoned for arriv ing at normative capacity. Submission of Form I (1) is essential. Similarly, for consideration of Cane Development Awards, normative capacity arrived at based on actual installed capacity shall be considered. Applications without copies of Form I (1) and R T 8 (C) shall not be considered for award under ‘Technical Efficiency Category’. 5. No factory shall be eligible for more than one award in a particular year. In case, a factory is found eligible awards in for more than onecategory, the sugar factory shall be considered for award in only one category as per the recommendation of Selection Committee. 6. For evaluation of overall performance sugar factory weightage for the marks obtained in various categories is given as under: a. Financial Management- 40% b. Cane Development - 30% c. Technical Efficiency - 30% 100% 7. Evaluation of financial performance shall be based on the figures indicated in the audited Balance Sheet and Profit & Loss Account of the sugar factory. Therefore, duly attested copies of previous two years’ audited balance sheets and Profit & Loss Statements shall be furnished with the application for award under ‘Finance Category’. Applications without audited accounts shall not be considered. 2 8. The number of awards in each category shall be as under: Sl. text: ANNEXURE-A Scheme for distribution of Efficiency Awards for the year 2023-24 1. Only those factories who have submitted application in the prescribed format will be considered eligible for participation. 2. The cooperative sugar factories, which are having any dues to NFCSF, will not be considered for awards. The applications shall be accompanied with ‘No Dues Certificate' obtained from NFCSF. 3. The factories have been categorized in two zones namely (a) High Recovery Area (HRA) having Sugar recovery 10% and abo ve and (b) Other Recovery Area (ORA) i.e. recovery below 10%. The States falling under these two categories are as under:- a. High Recovery Area (HRA) - South Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka. [Note: South Gujarat comprises districts of Surat, Valsad, Bh aruch and Narmada in Gujarat State]. b. Other Recovery Area (ORA) - Areas other than those specified at (a) above. 4. If the actual installed capacity of the sugar mill is more than the licensed capacity, the actual installed capacity shall be reckoned for arriv ing at normative capacity. Submission of Form I (1) is essential. Similarly, for consideration of Cane Development Awards, normative capacity arrived at based on actual installed capacity shall be considered. Applications without copies of Form I (1) and R T 8 (C) shall not be considered for award under ‘Technical Efficiency Category’. 5. No factory shall be eligible for more than one award in a particular year. In case, a factory is found eligible awards in for more than onecategory, the sugar factory shall be considered for award in only one category as per the recommendation of Selection Committee. 6. For evaluation of overall performance sugar factory weightage for the marks obtained in various categories is given as under: a. Financial Management- 40% b. Cane Development - 30% c. Technical Efficiency - 30% 100% 7. Evaluation of financial performance shall be based on the figures indicated in the audited Balance Sheet and Profit & Loss Account of the sugar factory. Supervise, direct and control the matters relating to preparation of electoral rolls; and iii. Such other functions as may be prescribed. 3. CEA ls responsible for preparation of electoral rolls consisting of individual eligible members or/and delegates/representatives as per MSCS Act and Rules framed thereunder and as per bye-laws, conduct of elections of Board of Directors and Office Bearers of the MSCS. 4 Section 45J(8) reads as follows: "The Chairperson and the Chief Executive of the Multi State Cooperative Society shall inform the Authority, six months before the expiry of the term of the existing board, to cottduct the elections within time". 5. As per Section 10(2)(ir) of the Act, the tenure of Directors, Chairperson and all the Office Bearers of the Society shall not exceed five (5) years. As per Section 45(5), the term of office bearers.shall be co-terminus with the term of Board. Therefore, continuation of the Board beyond the period as stipulated in the Act is without Authority. There is no provision for extension of the period of the Board in the Act. Therefore, it is essential to submit the request for conduct of election in time as well as to complete the entire. election process before expiry of the Board. ty to 1 CEO. lt is the duty of the CEO to follow up with the Cooperative Election Authori 6. Conduct of election and its completion of election process is not only the responsibility of the CEA but equally of the Society and the existing Chairperson and v^ furnish all the information/documents as required by CEA and get the election programme issued. 7. ln case of newly registered society, promoter members should conduct first general meeting within six months of the registration of the society (Rule 14) for the election of the board of directors and submit the request to CEA accordingly. 8. The following steps should be followed to submit the election request through the portal of CRCS (https.//crcs. qov. in). l. Log in to CRCS portal using the credentials (lD & Password) of the Society. Il. Navigate to the election request section. lll. Fill the required details completely and accurately in the respective field. lV. Attach following necessary document in the portal in PDF a) Election Request signed by Chairperson & CEOiMD of Society. b) Resolution of present Board of Directors to conduct election. c) Previous schedules of election of Members of Board of Directors and Office Bearers including proceedings of Returning Officers. d) Latest approved Bye-Laws of the Society. e) Fact sheet signed by Chairperson & CEO/MD of Society. V. Submit the request online 9. Providing incomplete information may lead to delays in finalization of election programme. Therefore, personal involvement and supervision of CEO is essential in this process. 10. This circular is issued in order to ensure free, fair and transparent conduct of election of MSCS in a timely manner. l/tz/2"> O\,!ivddi)(Ved Pra sh Assrstant Registrar Cooperative Election Authority u3* Copy to : 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 All the CEOs of MSCSS. No. 225/129/2022/ Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue (Central Board of Direct Taxes) ***** Circular No. 25/2022 New Delhi, Dated 30th December, 2022 Subject: Clarification for the purposes of clause (c) of Section 269ST of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in respect of dealership/distributorship contract in case of Co-operative Societies -reg. Section 269ST inter-alia prohibits receipt of an amount of two lakh rupees or more (hereinafter referred to as 'the prescribed limit') by a person, in the circumstances specified therein, through modes other than by way of an account payee cheque or an account payee bank draft or use of electronic clearing system through a bank account or through such other electronic mode as may be prescribed. 2. References have been received in respect of Milk Producers' Cooperative as to whether under the provisions of Section 269ST of the Act, receipt(s) in cash in a day of bank holiday/closure of bank day within 'the prescribed limit' from a distributor against sale of milk when payments were through bank on all other days is to be considered as a single transaction or whether all such receipts in cash in a previous year would be aggregated in respect of transactions with a distributor to treat it as one event or occasion. 3. With respect to the reference at Para 2 above, it is clarified that in respect of Co-operative Societies, a dealership/ distributorship contract by itself may not constitute an event or occasion for the purposes of clause ( c) of Section 269ST. Receipt related to such a dealership/distributorship contract by the Co-operative Society on any day in a previous year, which is within 'the prescribed limit' and complies with clause (a) as well as clause (b) of Section 269ST, may not be aggregated across multiple days for purposes of clause ( c) of Section 269ST for that previous year. -~ t>\\~'<-(,l-1- (Ravinder Maini) Director to the Government India Copy to: I.
